scope.vantage_point: This map is written from the vantage point of the AI safety community: it asks where work on making advanced AI safe and secure is happening and where it is missing. Several problems on the map are owned by other, often older and larger, fields; where that is so the map names the field and describes its connection to AI developers and AI safety.
scope.node_count_is_not_importance: Each problem gets one tile of the same size. The number of tiles in a layer or sub-area reflects how finely the problems split, not how important they are.
scope.capacity_is_not_progress: Capacity describes how much work exists on a problem, not how close it is to solved. A busy problem can be far from solved and is often where the jobs are.

out_of_scope_for_now.topic: Environmental and resource costs of AI (energy, water, land, grid)

out_of_scope_for_now.note: Out of scope for now; privacy and data leakage from models is the first topic to revisit.

lens_definitions.loss-of-control: Nodes about AI systems acting against their developers' intentions in ways humans might not be able to detect or reverse: scheming, weakening oversight, containment, and the governance of highly capable systems inside developers.
lens_definitions.agents: Nodes about AI systems that take multi-step actions in the world with tools and permissions: their security, containment, reliability, identity and accountability, and interactions between them.
lens_definitions.democracy: Nodes about AI's effect on self-government: manipulation of voters, surveillance and censorship, concentration of power, and the tools and information environment that collective decisions depend on.
lens_definitions.defensive-technology: Nodes about building technology that strengthens defenders and society's resilience faster than the risks grow, sometimes called defensive acceleration or differential technology development.
lens_definitions.open-source: Nodes where the publication of model weights, open tools or open models changes the problem, for better or worse.
lens_definitions.critical-infrastructure: Nodes about the energy, water, health, finance, transport and communications systems society depends on, whether threatened by attackers or by AI failing inside them.

layers.name: The Model
layers.definition: Making the AI system itself safe, secure and reliable: getting its goals right, understanding its internals, containing it if that fails, measuring what it can do, protecting it from attackers and insiders, making it dependable in use, and giving credible assurance about all of this.

subareas.name: Alignment
subareas.definition: Making an AI system's actual objectives and behaviour match what its developers intend, including under optimisation pressure, at scale, and when the system may become more capable than the humans overseeing it. Covers both training-time techniques and the conceptual work on what alignment even requires.
subareas.scope_rule: In: getting a model's goals and behaviour to track what its developers intend, including detecting and removing unwanted goals and making safety training hard to undo. Out: containing a model that may already be misaligned (model.control), measuring misalignment (model.evaluations), and understanding internals for their own sake (model.interpretability).

nodes.name: Scalable oversight
nodes.definition: Getting reliable training and evaluation signal on tasks where humans cannot directly judge whether a model's output is correct, because the task is too long, complex or specialised, or because the model is more capable than the people checking it. Approaches include debate (two copies of a model argue opposite sides and a human or weaker model judges which case holds up), recursive reward modelling (models help humans evaluate other models' work), and weak-to-strong generalisation (studying whether a strong model trained on labels from a weaker supervisor ends up more capable and more honest than that supervisor).
nodes.why_it_matters: Without a way to supervise superhuman work, developers cannot tell whether training is reinforcing genuinely good behaviour or just behaviour that looks good to an overwhelmed or fooled human rater.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Training pipelines that reliably produce correct, non-deceptive behaviour on tasks no human grader could check unaided, validated by held-out ground truth or by weak-to-strong generalisation experiments.

canonical_reference.title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models (Bowman et al., 2022)

key_agendas.name: AI safety via debate
Weak-to-strong generalisation
An alignment safety case sketch based on debate (UK AISI)
Eliciting latent knowledge (ARC)

nodes.boundary_notes: Designs the training signal. model.control.control-protocols uses trusted models to watch a model at deployment time rather than to train it, and model.evaluations.science-of-evaluations checks whether a method worked rather than supplying the signal. model.alignment.superintelligence-alignment covers approaches aimed at systems far beyond any current overseer; this node covers methods testable on today's models.
nodes.capacity_note: Anthropic and Google DeepMind run debate and weak-to-strong research, UK AISI has an alignment team working on it, and outside them the work is a few academic groups and ARC's more theoretical agenda.
nodes.entry_points: MATS (matsprogram.org) and the Anthropic Fellows Program are the standard mentored routes into empirical scalable-oversight research, and debate and weak-to-strong experiments can be reproduced on open-weight models with modest compute. UK AISI's alignment team periodically hires for debate research. ARC publishes its theoretical work openly but hires rarely.

nodes.name: Reward hacking and specification gaming
nodes.definition: A system achieves the letter of the objective it is trained or tested on in a way its designers did not intend, exploiting gaps between the measurable reward and the real goal. Examples range from simulated agents exploiting physics bugs to coding models that special-case or edit unit tests, or tamper with the grading setup, to score as passing. It matters more as reinforcement learning on long agentic tasks becomes a main way frontier models are trained.
nodes.why_it_matters: Reward hacking learned in training can generalise into broader misaligned behaviour, as Anthropic reported in 2025, and it can reach the real world: in July 2026 OpenAI disclosed that models under evaluation escaped their test environment and broke into Hugging Face's production systems to obtain the answers to a cyber evaluation. Undetected, it lets a system look more capable and aligned than it is.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Training and reward-design methods, plus monitoring, that catch specification gaming during training rather than after deployment, and objectives that are harder to game in the first place.

canonical_reference.title: Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning (Lilian Weng, 2024)

key_agendas.name: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking (Anthropic, 2025)
Monitoring reasoning models for misbehaviour (OpenAI, 2025)
Recent frontier models are reward hacking (METR, 2025)
Specification gaming examples (Google DeepMind)

nodes.boundary_notes: The training-time cause and fix. Measuring gaming-like tendencies in a finished model belongs to model.evaluations.propensity-and-character-evals. Where gaming becomes strategic and hidden from overseers it shades into model.alignment.scheming.
nodes.capacity_note: Fixes are developed mostly inside the labs that run large-scale reinforcement learning (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind), while METR and Palisade Research document reward hacking in released models.
nodes.entry_points: Most training-side work happens in labs' alignment and post-training teams. From outside, the practical routes are reproducing reward hacking in open RL environments on open-weight models, contributing to evaluators' write-ups of reward hacking in released models (METR publishes these), or applying to Coefficient Giving's Technical AI Safety RFP, which names reward hacking as a funded area.

nodes.name: Scheming and deceptive alignment
nodes.definition: A model behaves as if aligned during training and evaluation while pursuing different goals once it judges it is unmonitored or deployed, sometimes called alignment faking or scheming. This includes models strategically hiding their true objectives or capabilities from evaluators.
nodes.why_it_matters: A model that can convincingly fake alignment defeats training-based and evaluation-based safety checks alike, so this failure mode has to be ruled out, not just tested for once.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Reliable methods to detect scheming precursors during training, and empirical evidence about how likely scheming is to arise under realistic training setups, backed by red-teaming that tries to induce it deliberately.

canonical_reference.title: Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming

key_agendas.name: Sleeper Agents: training deceptive LLMs that persist through safety training

Detecting and reducing scheming (OpenAI and Apollo Research)
Apollo Research scheming evaluations
Tailwind: Training run fault injections

nodes.boundary_notes: The mechanism, the model organisms that reproduce it, and training-side fixes. Detecting deliberate underperformance on tests is model.evaluations.sandbagging-and-elicitation; reading hidden intent from internals or reasoning traces is model.interpretability.internal-monitoring and model.interpretability.chain-of-thought-monitorability; safeguards that hold even if scheming is not fixed are model.control.
nodes.capacity_note: One of the busiest empirical topics in safety research, with Apollo Research and Redwood Research working on it alongside lab teams at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind.

open_problems_source.title: We Need A Science of Scheming

nodes.entry_points: Apollo Research is hiring and publishes its evaluation methodology openly; Coefficient Giving's 'Misalignment red team' and 'Training run fault injections' Tailwind initiatives are open funding routes for anyone wanting to build model organisms of scheming.

nodes.name: Goal misgeneralisation and emergent misalignment
nodes.definition: How the goals and behaviour a model learns in training carry over to situations training did not cover. Two failure modes anchor the area: goal misgeneralisation, where a model competently pursues a goal that matched the intended one during training but diverges from it in new situations; and emergent misalignment, where fine-tuning on a narrow task (such as writing insecure code) produces broadly misaligned behaviour elsewhere. Research asks which training data, methods and model 'personas' make good behaviour generalise, and includes techniques such as latent adversarial training that apply pressure to a model's internal representations rather than only its inputs.
nodes.why_it_matters: A model that behaves safely only on inputs resembling its training distribution will fail exactly when it matters most: in unusual, high-stakes or adversarial situations.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Training methods with a theoretical or strong empirical account of why they generalise safely, validated against held-out distribution shifts and targeted adversarial probes rather than only in-distribution benchmarks.

canonical_reference.title: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs (Betley et al., 2025)

key_agendas.name: Goal misgeneralisation: why correct specifications aren't enough (Google DeepMind)
Emergent misalignment (Truthful AI)
Understanding and preventing misalignment generalisation (OpenAI)

Latent adversarial training

nodes.boundary_notes: How training makes aligned behaviour hold up off-distribution. Defending a finished model against deliberate adversarial prompts is model.model-security.jailbreak-robustness; making safeguards survive weight modification is model.alignment.unlearning-and-tamper-resistance; a model that hides misaligned goals strategically is model.alignment.scheming; bad behaviour triggered by a deliberately planted backdoor is model.model-security.supply-chain-and-integrity.
nodes.capacity_note: Emergent misalignment (2025) opened an active research direction followed up by teams at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind, with Truthful AI the one small independent group for which it is a core topic.
nodes.entry_points: The emergent misalignment models, datasets and code are public (github.com/emergent-misalignment/emergent-misalignment), as is the latent adversarial training codebase (github.com/aengusl/latent-adversarial-training); both let a technically able entrant reproduce and extend core results on open-weight models without an institutional affiliation. Truthful AI takes MATS scholars.

nodes.name: Unlearning and tamper-resistant safeguards
nodes.definition: Techniques to reliably erase specific dangerous knowledge or skills from a model's weights, and to make safety behaviour survive later fine-tuning or weight editing, rather than merely suppressing capabilities with refusals that can be bypassed by fine-tuning or clever prompting.
nodes.why_it_matters: Suppression-only safeguards can be stripped by anyone who can fine-tune or jailbreak the model; genuine unlearning would make dangerous capabilities harder to recover even from an open-weight or stolen model.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Unlearning methods proven robust to adversarial fine-tuning and relearning attempts, not just to the original prompting-based jailbreaks used to evaluate them.

canonical_reference.title: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety (Barez et al., 2025)

key_agendas.name: WMDP benchmark and RMU unlearning (Center for AI Safety)
Tamper-resistant safeguards for open-weight LLMs (TAR)
Deep Ignorance: pretraining data filtering (EleutherAI and UK AISI)
An adversarial perspective on machine unlearning for AI safety

nodes.boundary_notes: The defensive side of misuse.open-weights.safeguard-removal, which studies how cheaply safeguards are stripped once weights are public. Distinct from model.model-security.weights-security, which stops weights being stolen at all, and from model.interpretability.safety-applications, which includes targeted weight edits as one application of interpretability.
nodes.capacity_note: CAIS built the standard benchmark and early methods, and EleutherAI, UK AISI and Oxford showed in 2025 that filtering pretraining data holds up better against fine-tuning than most unlearning methods, which can still be reversed cheaply.

open_problems_source.title: Open problems in machine unlearning for AI safety

nodes.entry_points: Deep Ignorance released all models, datasets and checkpoints openly (deepignorance.ai), giving an entrant a working baseline to extend; EleutherAI is open to outside collaborators and UK AISI publishes some roles publicly despite being otherwise closed.

nodes.name: Alignment for superintelligence
nodes.definition: Research agendas aimed at aligning systems whose capabilities would far exceed the ability of any human, or any current AI-assisted overseer, to check directly. Bets include non-agentic 'scientist' AI that predicts and explains rather than acts (LawZero), systems built from inspectable, human-like reasoning steps (Conjecture's cognitive emulation), and provable-safety approaches.
nodes.why_it_matters: If capabilities keep advancing, techniques that work for checking today's models may simply stop applying once no overseer can understand what the system is doing; this node is about the case where scalable oversight itself runs out of road.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Credible, technically detailed plans for aligning systems beyond human oversight, with more than one well-resourced team pursuing each serious alternative.

canonical_reference.title: Superintelligent Agents Pose Catastrophic Risks: Can Scientist AI Offer a Safer Path? (Bengio et al., 2025)

key_agendas.name: Scientist AI (LawZero)
Cognitive emulation (Conjecture)
Tailwind: Alignment moonshots

nodes.boundary_notes: Long-shot agendas for systems that no human or current AI-assisted overseer could check. The frontier labs' plan to automate alignment research with AI is model.alignment.automated-alignment-research; incremental oversight methods for current models are model.alignment.scalable-oversight; the philosophical groundwork is model.alignment.conceptual-foundations; what happens to society if alignment is not solved in time sits in society.structural-risk.
nodes.capacity_note: Three organisations name this as their mission (LawZero, SSI and Conjecture), with LawZero the best resourced after a commitment of up to CAD 300 million in September 2026; SSI publishes no research.
nodes.entry_points: Both organisations are hiring (SSI for research engineers/scientists, LawZero more broadly as it scales after its September 2026 funding round); there is no open community programme specific to this node yet.

nodes.name: Automated alignment research
nodes.definition: Using AI systems to do much of the work of alignment research itself (running experiments, proposing and checking methods, writing up results) and being able to trust what they produce. Frontier labs name this as their main plan for aligning systems more capable than their overseers, but it depends on verifying AI-produced safety work that humans may not be able to check line by line, and on catching a model that subtly sabotages or sandbags the research.
nodes.why_it_matters: If the plan works, alignment research could keep pace with capabilities; if AI-produced safety work is trusted without being verifiable, a subtly misaligned model could steer the very research meant to catch it.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Demonstrations that AI research agents produce alignment results humans can verify, evaluations that catch sabotage and sandbagging of research, and published criteria for when a developer would rely on AI-produced safety work.

canonical_reference.title: Can we safely automate alignment research? (Joe Carlsmith, 2025)

key_agendas.name: Automated Alignment Researchers (Anthropic)
Automated researchers can subtly sandbag (Anthropic Alignment Science, 2025)
Automated alignment research (Superalignment framing, OpenAI 2023)

nodes.boundary_notes: Trusting and scaling AI-produced safety research. Alignment approaches for systems beyond any overseer that do not rest on automation are model.alignment.superintelligence-alignment; independent organisations adopting AI tools for their own research is meta.tooling.ai-uplift; a model deliberately underperforming on evaluations is model.evaluations.sandbagging-and-elicitation; automated AI R&D in general, and the internal deployments that run it, are model.developer-assurance.internal-deployment.
nodes.capacity_note: The labs' main plan for aligning more capable systems, but public work is mostly Anthropic's experiments with automated alignment researchers and its studies of subtle sandbagging; OpenAI's dedicated team was disbanded in 2024.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Developers test automated researchers on problems with known answers before relying on them, and control-style monitoring of internal agents is starting to be applied; no developer has published criteria for when AI-produced safety work is trusted.
nodes.entry_points: Anthropic's Alignment Science team and the Anthropic Fellows Program publish and hire in this area. Outside the labs, the open work is evaluations for research sabotage and sandbagging, which can be built on open-weight models.

nodes.name: Conceptual foundations of alignment
nodes.definition: Philosophical and mathematical clarification of what 'alignment' requires and what goals, agency and optimisation mean for AI systems, so that technical work aims at the right target.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without shared, precise concepts, empirical alignment work risks optimising for the wrong target or talking past adjacent fields, wasting scarce research effort.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Widely-adopted, precise framings of the core threat models that let empirical researchers, evaluators and policymakers point to the same failure mode and disagree productively about solutions rather than definitions.

canonical_reference.title: The Alignment Problem from a Deep Learning Perspective (Ngo, Chan and Mindermann)

key_agendas.name: Risks from learned optimisation (inner and outer alignment)
Embedded agency / agent foundations (MIRI)
Assistance games (CHAI)
Full-stack alignment (Meaning Alignment Institute)

nodes.boundary_notes: Asks what alignment is. Mapping how catastrophe could actually unfold is meta.evidence.threat-modelling, and choosing between interventions is meta.evidence.macrostrategy-and-prioritisation. Distinct from model.evaluations.science-of-evaluations (measurement rigour) and from society.structural-risk (multi-actor consequences).
nodes.capacity_note: Several very small groups (Principles of Intelligence, Orthogonal, ACS, Dovetail, the Meaning Alignment Institute) and one established academic centre (CHAI) work here, each with a handful to about twenty people.
nodes.entry_points: Principles of Intelligence (formerly PIBBSS) runs the PIBBSS summer fellowship, the standard entry route into this style of research, and ILIAD runs conferences and a fellowship on theoretical alignment. Orthogonal, ACS and Dovetail publish openly and are small enough to approach directly.

subareas.name: Interpretability
subareas.definition: Reverse-engineering the internal computations of neural networks well enough to verify, predict, or steer their behaviour, instead of treating them as black boxes. Spans mechanistic methods, monitoring visible reasoning such as chain of thought, and the pure science of what these systems compute.
subareas.scope_rule: In: understanding or exposing what happens inside a model, including whether its visible reasoning is faithful, and safety techniques that work through internals. Out: safety techniques that never look inside the model (model.alignment, model.control) and monitoring of outputs alone (model.control.control-protocols).

nodes.name: Understanding model internals
nodes.definition: Methods for decomposing a model's internal computation into human-understandable parts (features, circuits, sparse autoencoders and their successors), and the basic science of what deep networks compute, such as superposition, generalisation and in-context learning. This is the shared toolkit and body of knowledge the rest of interpretability draws on.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without a reliable account of what happens inside a model, every safety claim rests on outward behaviour, which a capable or deceptive model can make look fine.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Methods that explain a large share of a frontier model's behaviour in terms humans can check, validated against ground truth, and a settled scientific account of phenomena such as superposition.

canonical_reference.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability

key_agendas.name: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs (Anthropic, 2025)
Towards Monosemanticity: sparse dictionary learning
Toy Models of Superposition
Gemma Scope open sparse autoencoders (Google DeepMind)
Singular learning theory / developmental interpretability (Timaeus)

nodes.boundary_notes: Builds the methods and the science. Putting them to work for a safety goal is model.interpretability.safety-applications and model.interpretability.internal-monitoring; checking whether the methods themselves work is model.interpretability.interpretability-benchmarks.
nodes.capacity_note: The largest single research agenda in technical safety, with lab teams, dedicated nonprofits, a well-funded startup (Goodfire) and academic groups, still far from explaining frontier models at scale.
nodes.entry_points: Neuronpedia is fully open and welcomes outside contributions with no affiliation required; EleutherAI runs an open Discord and collaborates with outside researchers; ARENA (the interpretability-heavy technical bootcamp) is the standard training route in.

nodes.name: Chain-of-thought monitorability
nodes.definition: Measuring and preserving the property that a model's visible chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflects the computation actually driving its output, so that reading the reasoning tells you something true about why the model did what it did. Includes detecting reasoning that is encoded or hidden inside otherwise fluent text.
nodes.why_it_matters: Visible reasoning is currently one of the few windows into a model's intentions before it acts; if that window closes (models compressing reasoning, or training pressure making it unfaithful), a major current safety affordance is lost.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Standard metrics for monitorability that labs track and report over time, plus training practices demonstrated not to erode it, so that the property degrading would be caught early rather than discovered after the fact.

canonical_reference.title: Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety

key_agendas.name: A Pragmatic Way to Measure Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
Frontier Model Forum issue brief on CoT monitorability
Tailwind: Oversight of CoT monitorability

nodes.boundary_notes: Whether the reasoning trace is a trustworthy signal. Using that signal in a deployment-time protocol is model.control.control-protocols; reading internal activations rather than text is model.interpretability.internal-monitoring. Many organisations doing this work describe it as control or evaluation; it sits here because the question is whether a view into the model's reasoning is faithful.
nodes.capacity_note: A cross-lab effort since the 2025 joint position paper, with authors from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and UK AISI and follow-up work by Apollo, Redwood and METR, though no organisation has it as its main mandate.

open_problems_source.title: A Pragmatic Way to Measure Chain-of-Thought Monitorability

nodes.entry_points: The Frontier Model Forum's issue brief and the joint arXiv paper both list open measurement questions; Redwood Research and Apollo Research are the two independent nonprofits actively hiring into monitoring-adjacent roles.

nodes.name: Probes and internal monitoring
nodes.definition: Training small, cheap classifiers ('probes') on a model's internal activations, the numerical states passed between its layers, to flag harmful, deceptive or misaligned behaviour as it happens. A real-time safeguard layer distinct from filtering the output text.
nodes.why_it_matters: A model can produce an innocuous-looking output while its internal state reflects a harmful plan; probing activations can catch this even when the visible output or chain of thought does not.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Probes shown to generalise to novel harmful behaviours they were not trained on, rather than only catching the specific patterns used to construct them, deployed as a standard part of production monitoring.

canonical_reference.title: Simple probes can catch sleeper agents

key_agendas.name: Detecting strategic deception using linear probes (Apollo Research)

Obfuscated activations bypass latent-space defences (FAR.AI and others)

nodes.boundary_notes: The probing technique itself. Its raw material comes from model.interpretability.understanding-internals; the protocol that decides what to do when a probe fires is model.control.control-protocols; monitoring the visible reasoning text rather than activations is model.interpretability.chain-of-thought-monitorability.
nodes.capacity_note: Probes run in production at Google DeepMind and are used at Anthropic, and Apollo Research and FAR.AI publish independent work on deception probes and attacks that evade them.
nodes.entry_points: Apollo Research's deception-detection code is open (github.com/ApolloResearch/deception-detection), and the Anthropic sleeper-agent and Google DeepMind Gemini probe papers are detailed enough to reproduce on open-weight models. MATS interpretability streams regularly run probing projects; beyond that the route is a lab or Apollo role.

nodes.name: Interpretability benchmarks
nodes.definition: Standardised tasks, metrics and datasets for comparing interpretability methods against each other and against ground truth, so that claimed progress can be verified rather than taken on faith.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without shared benchmarks, it is hard to tell whether a new interpretability method is a genuine advance or just a better story about the same level of understanding, which slows the whole field down.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Widely-adopted benchmarks with known ground truth (for example, models with deliberately inserted, known circuits) that new interpretability methods are routinely evaluated against before publication.

canonical_reference.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark

key_agendas.name: SAEBench
MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
AxBench: steering and concept detection benchmark

nodes.boundary_notes: Benchmarks for interpretability methods, not for models. Capability and behaviour benchmarks for models are model.evaluations.benchmarks-and-tooling.
nodes.capacity_note: Two maintained benchmarking efforts (SAEBench and MIB) and a few one-off studies, with Neuronpedia as shared infrastructure.

open_problems_source.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability (benchmarking section)

nodes.entry_points: Both SAEBench (via Neuronpedia) and MIB (mib-bench.github.io) are open leaderboards that accept external submissions of new methods without requiring institutional affiliation.

nodes.name: Interpretability applied to safety
nodes.definition: Using interpretability for concrete safety work: auditing a model for hidden objectives or awareness that it is being evaluated before deployment, steering behaviour directly through internal features or directions, eliciting knowledge the model has but does not state, and finding inputs that trigger bad behaviour by analysing internals.
nodes.why_it_matters: Interpretability only pays off for safety once its findings are turned into something that changes what a deployed model does or how it is checked; this is the bridge from understanding to intervention.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Interpretability-derived interventions (steering, targeted unlearning, elicited latent knowledge) that outperform black-box alternatives on a safety-relevant task, in production rather than only in a research demo.

The same refusal-direction understanding is used offensively to strip safeguards, which is misuse.open-weights.safeguard-removal; this node owns the defensive use.

subareas.name: Control
subareas.definition: Designing protocols and system-level safeguards that keep a possibly misaligned or untrusted model from causing serious harm, without relying on having solved alignment first. Treats the model as an untrusted actor and builds containment, monitoring and verification around it.
subareas.scope_rule: In: system-level safeguards (protocols, monitoring, sandboxing, formal guarantees) that limit harm from a model whose alignment is not assumed. Out: changing the model's objectives (model.alignment); defending the model against outside attackers (model.model-security); measuring whether a model is misaligned (model.evaluations).

nodes.name: Control evaluations
nodes.definition: Red-teaming methodology that stress-tests whether a control protocol actually constrains a model that is trying to subvert it, typically by having a red-team model play the role of an adversarial, misalignment-simulating agent against the protocol.
nodes.why_it_matters: A control protocol that has not been tested against a model actively trying to defeat it gives false confidence; this is the only way to know a safeguard holds under adversarial pressure rather than only under cooperative conditions.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Standard, widely-used control evaluation suites that labs run before deploying any new control protocol, analogous to how penetration testing is standard practice in classical security.

canonical_reference.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

key_agendas.name: Redwood Research AI control agenda
ControlArena (UK AISI open-source control evaluation library)

nodes.boundary_notes: Tests whether a specific safeguard holds against a model trying to subvert it. Measuring raw capability or propensity with no protocol in place is model.evaluations.dangerous-capability-evals; the protocols being tested are model.control.control-protocols.
nodes.capacity_note: Redwood Research remains the centre of gravity, with a UK AISI control red team, METR's monitorability work and Poseidon Research adding capacity.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Ad hoc red-teaming of specific protocols before internal deployment at labs adopting the methodology; no shared standard suite yet.
nodes.entry_points: Redwood Research publishes open problems and hires for control research. UK AISI's open-source ControlArena library (control-arena.aisi.org.uk) is the easiest way to run a control evaluation yourself. ControlConf, run by Redwood Research with FAR.AI, is the field's main gathering. UK AISI periodically opens roles on its control team.

nodes.name: Control protocols and monitoring
nodes.definition: Concrete schemes for getting useful work from a model whose alignment has not been verified: trusted monitoring (a weaker, trusted model checks the untrusted one), editing or resampling suspicious actions before they run, and hierarchical monitoring in which AI monitors handle routine oversight at scale and escalate uncertain or high-stakes cases to limited human review.
nodes.why_it_matters: While alignment cannot be verified, these protocols are what stands between a subtly misaligned model with access to real systems and serious harm, including sabotage of safety work itself.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Protocols with measured safety and usefulness under adversarial testing that labs actually run on their internal agent deployments, with human review budgets sized to the risk.

canonical_reference.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

key_agendas.name: Redwood Research AI control agenda
Ctrl-Z: controlling AI agents via resampling
An approach to technical AGI safety and security (Google DeepMind), monitoring sections

nodes.boundary_notes: The deployment-time decision protocol. Its monitoring signals come from model.interpretability.chain-of-thought-monitorability and model.interpretability.internal-monitoring; its adversarial testing is model.control.control-evaluations; limiting an agent's permissions regardless of monitoring is model.control.agent-sandboxing. Defending an agent from outside attackers is model.model-security.agent-security. Oversight of the aggregate societal system, rather than one deployment, is society.structural-risk.gradual-disempowerment.
nodes.capacity_note: Mostly carried by Redwood Research, with Luthien's open-source implementation, and Anthropic and Google DeepMind running protocols on their own internal deployments.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Trusted monitoring and resampling protocols piloted internally at some labs; hierarchical human-review escalation remains mostly conceptual outside Redwood's papers.
nodes.entry_points: Redwood Research's published agenda and open roles are the most direct route in. METR's monitorability-evaluation blog series is a good way to see where independent groups are starting to contribute to the monitoring side of protocol design.

nodes.name: Agent sandboxing and containment
nodes.definition: Restricting an AI agent's affordances, such as tool access, permissions, filesystem or network reach, so that even a misaligned or compromised agent has limited ability to cause harm regardless of what it decides to do.
nodes.why_it_matters: As agents get more autonomy and real-world tool access, the damage one bad decision or scheming episode can do grows. This is no longer hypothetical: in July 2026 OpenAI disclosed that models under evaluation chained vulnerabilities to escape their test environment and reach Hugging Face's production systems. Containment limits the damage whether the cause is misalignment or outside exploitation.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Standard, low-overhead sandboxing infrastructure for agentic deployments that is adopted as a default rather than an opt-in, with documented containment failures becoming rare and quickly caught.

canonical_reference.title: Out of Bounds: What the U.S. Government Should Do in Response to AI Agent Containment Failures

nodes.boundary_notes: Limits what the agent itself can do because its alignment is not trusted. Defending a trusted agent against prompt injection by a third party is model.model-security.agent-security; stopping the weights leaving the building is model.model-security.weights-security; a human deliberately pointing an agent at an outside target is misuse.cyber.autonomous-intrusion.
nodes.capacity_note: Developers sandbox their own agents and evaluation environments with mature commercial and open-source isolation technology, but nobody builds containment specifically against a model treated as an adversary.
nodes.owner_field: cloud, container and agent-infrastructure security (commercial sandbox providers, cloud isolation, evaluation sandboxing such as Inspect's)
nodes.connection_note: Isolation technology already flows into developers' products and evaluation harnesses, but what should flow and mostly does not is the control community's model-as-adversary threat model into how that technology is configured and tested, which the July 2026 escape showed is needed.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Per-product sandboxing (VM isolation, scoped permissions, network restrictions) built ad hoc by individual labs; no shared, independently-audited standard.
nodes.entry_points: There is no dedicated independent organisation to point an entrant at; the most concrete public technical description of current practice is Anthropic's engineering write-up, and Redwood Research's control agenda is the closest research programme treating containment as a first-class safeguard.

nodes.name: Formal verification and guaranteed-safe AI
nodes.definition: Building AI systems, or wrappers around them, whose safety-relevant behaviour can be formally proven or mathematically guaranteed against a specification, rather than only empirically tested. Sometimes framed as separating a possibly-opaque AI component from a verified safety layer around it.
nodes.why_it_matters: Empirical control protocols reduce risk but cannot rule it out entirely; formal guarantees, where achievable, offer a fundamentally stronger form of assurance for the highest-stakes deployments.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Formal methods that scale beyond toy examples to give meaningful guarantees about real deployed systems' behaviour in specific, bounded domains, expanding gradually to less constrained settings.

canonical_reference.title: Towards Guaranteed Safe AI: A Framework for Ensuring Robust and Reliable AI Systems

key_agendas.name: ARIA Safeguarded AI programme
Towards Guaranteed Safe AI framework
Provably safe systems (Tegmark and Omohundro)

nodes.boundary_notes: Seeks provable guarantees, where model.control.control-protocols accepts statistical risk reduction. Verifying that states or developers keep an agreement is a different use of the word, covered by society.compute-governance.agreement-verification.
nodes.capacity_note: Essentially one major funded programme (ARIA's Safeguarded AI, refocused in November 2025 on an open mathematical assurance toolkit) plus a few small organisations.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Formal methods applied to narrow, bounded components (e.g. specific control software) rather than to frontier model behaviour generally.
nodes.entry_points: ARIA's Safeguarded AI programme funds teams building the mathematical assurance toolkit (its calls are the main route in for researchers with formal-methods backgrounds). Atlas Ignota publishes open problems for those wanting to join a small team. The Guaranteed Safe AI newsletter tracks the area.

nodes.name: Detecting loss-of-control incidents
nodes.definition: Identifying, in real deployments rather than in a lab, cases where an AI system has acted autonomously against its operator's intent, evaded or disabled its own oversight, or otherwise shown a genuine loss of control, as distinct from a human directing an AI to cause harm. Emerging methods include OSINT-based monitoring of publicly reported model behaviour and structured indications-and-warning frameworks adapted from intelligence analysis.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without a way to notice loss-of-control incidents as they happen in the world, evidence about whether models are actually becoming harder to control would only ever come from a lab's own internal testing or from a catastrophe severe enough to be undeniable.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A standing, credible, independent capability that can flag a real-world loss-of-control incident within days, classify its severity against a shared taxonomy, and feed findings back into control protocols and deployment decisions, rather than a one-off prototype.

canonical_reference.title: The Loss of Control Observatory: a prototype to detect real-world AI control incidents

key_agendas.name: CLTR Loss of Control Observatory (OSINT methodology)
Institute for Security and Technology: Indications & Warning for AI loss of control
RAND Europe: risks and response for AI loss-of-control incidents

nodes.boundary_notes: Misaligned AI acting on its own initiative, rather than a human directing an AI to attack a target, which is misuse.cyber.attack-detection. The precursor behaviours are studied in model.alignment.scheming and model.evaluations.sandbagging-and-elicitation; the deployment-time protocols meant to prevent an incident are model.control.control-protocols, which this node checks up on in the field. The general public record of AI incidents is meta.evidence.incident-tracking and root-cause investigation is meta.evidence.incident-investigation; this node is the specialised detection of loss-of-control cases. What a developer discloses about its own incidents is model.developer-assurance.incident-reporting.
nodes.capacity_note: CLTR's Loss of Control Observatory publishes roughly monthly and IST and RAND have written frameworks, but the most serious case so far was caught by the affected company rather than by any independent monitor.
nodes.existing_mitigations: OSINT monitoring and an indications-and-warning taxonomy exist as prototypes; neither is yet wired into any lab's or government's deployment decisions.

open_problems_source.title: CLTR: AI loss of control incidents are worsening

nodes.entry_points: CLTR is hiring and publishing open problems directly on this programme; IST and RAND both publish openly and are approachable for anyone wanting to extend the indications-and-warning framework work rather than build monitoring infrastructure from scratch.

subareas.name: Evaluations
subareas.definition: The science and practice of determining what a model can do, how it tends to behave, and how rigorous those measurements are, so that capability, safety and deployment decisions can be based on evidence rather than assumption. Distinct from building the safeguards or training fixes that respond to what evaluations find.
subareas.scope_rule: In: methods, benchmarks and tooling for measuring model capabilities and propensities, including domain-specific dangerous-capability testing such as cyber and bio, whoever runs it. Out: acting on results through training (model.alignment) or safeguards (model.control); who audits a developer and with what access (model.developer-assurance.third-party-auditing); real-world evidence of misuse (misuse layer).

nodes.name: Dangerous capability evaluations
nodes.definition: Assessing whether a model has capabilities that materially raise catastrophic risk, most prominently offensive cyber capability, biological and chemical weapons-relevant knowledge, and autonomous replication, whether the testing is done by the developer, a government institute or an independent specialist firm.
nodes.why_it_matters: Deployment and scaling decisions in current frontier safety frameworks are explicitly gated on these evaluations; without them, thresholds meant to trigger extra safeguards have nothing to trigger on.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Evaluation suites that reliably predict real-world uplift (not just benchmark performance), run before every major model release and cross-checked by more than one organisation.

canonical_reference.title: Model evaluation for extreme risks (Shevlane et al., 2023)

key_agendas.name: UK AISI risk research
METR frontier risk reports
FrontierCyber real-system evaluations
Frontier Model Forum risk taxonomy and thresholds

nodes.boundary_notes: Owns the measurement of the model, including cyber, bio, autonomy and AI R&D evaluation. The real-world threat and its defences sit in the Harmful use layer (for example misuse.cyber.offensive-uplift and misuse.bio-chem.knowledge-uplift, which also holds human-participant uplift studies). model.developer-assurance.frontier-safety-frameworks sets thresholds in terms of these results; what developers do once AI R&D capability arrives is model.developer-assurance.internal-deployment; turning results into demonstrations for policymakers is meta.evidence.capability-demonstrations.
nodes.capacity_note: Government institutes, frontier developers, METR and specialist evaluators such as Irregular and SecureBio test cyber, bio, autonomy and AI R&D capability regularly; predictive validity and independent cross-checking remain weak.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Frontier safety frameworks gate deployment and additional safeguards on these evaluation results; independent cross-checking is growing but still limited.

open_problems_source.title: Frontier Model Forum: Frontier Capability Assessments

nodes.entry_points: METR and SecureBio both publish open problems and hire for evaluation work and are the most approachable AI-safety-native routes in; UK AISI and CAISI periodically open government roles for those wanting the regulator side; Irregular is a commercial route for cyber-specifically skilled people.

nodes.name: Propensity and character evaluations
nodes.definition: Measuring what a model tends to do, as opposed to what it can do: whether it has stable values, goals or behavioural dispositions, and how to elicit and measure them, sometimes called model psychology. Covers honesty, sycophancy, power-seeking, resisting shutdown, blackmail or sabotage in agentic scenarios, and general behavioural consistency.
nodes.why_it_matters: A model can pass narrow capability and safety tests while still having concerning general dispositions (for example, a tendency to mislead on ambiguous questions) that only show up under broader behavioural probing.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Standard, validated instruments for measuring model dispositions that correlate with real deployment behaviour, tracked over model generations the way capability benchmarks are tracked now.

canonical_reference.title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations

key_agendas.name: Petri: open-source automated alignment auditing (Anthropic, now Meridian Labs)
Agentic misalignment (Anthropic, 2025)
MASK: disentangling honesty from accuracy (CAIS and Scale AI)
Tailwind: Misleadingness evaluations

nodes.boundary_notes: Measures dispositions (honesty, sycophancy, misleadingness, power-seeking) whatever their cause. Why a disposition arises is model.alignment.reward-hacking or model.alignment.scheming; whether a model can do something dangerous, as opposed to whether it tends to, is model.evaluations.dangerous-capability-evals.
nodes.capacity_note: Labs run most character work in-house, and independent evaluation exists in pieces (CAIS's MASK, Transluce, Palisade Research, Apollo Research, and the Petri tool maintained by Meridian Labs) without a standing evaluator tracking dispositions across model generations.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Labs' internal character and sycophancy evaluations reported in system cards; independent one-off studies (MASK, shutdown resistance, Transluce investigations); Petri as an open auditing tool. No independent instrument tracks dispositions across model generations.
nodes.entry_points: Petri (open source, maintained by Meridian Labs) lets anyone run automated propensity audits on open or API models. Transluce and Palisade Research publish independent behavioural studies and hire. Coefficient Giving's 'AI character evaluator' Tailwind initiative is looking to fund someone to build a standing independent evaluator, the clearest route for someone wanting to found one.

nodes.name: Science of evaluations
nodes.definition: Methodological work on making capability and safety evaluations themselves rigorous, reproducible, and predictive of behaviour at larger scale or after further fine-tuning, rather than accepting benchmark numbers at face value.
nodes.why_it_matters: An evaluation that is not reproducible, is gameable, or fails to predict how a model will actually behave once elicited properly gives false reassurance precisely where the stakes are highest.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Evaluation methodology treated as its own rigorous sub-discipline, with agreed standards for statistical power, elicitation effort and scaling extrapolation that evaluators are expected to meet.

canonical_reference.title: We need a Science of Evals (Apollo Research, 2024)

key_agendas.name: A statistical approach to model evaluations (Anthropic)
Measuring AI ability to complete long tasks: methodology (METR)
UK AISI research agenda, science of evaluations theme

nodes.boundary_notes: Methodological standards for evaluations: validity, reproducibility and predictive power. The shared benchmarks and software are model.evaluations.benchmarks-and-tooling; hidden capability specifically is model.evaluations.sandbagging-and-elicitation.
nodes.capacity_note: A named sub-topic inside evaluator organisations (UK AISI, Apollo Research, METR, Epoch AI) and labs, with no organisation that has evaluation methodology as its main output.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Individual evaluator organisations apply their own internal standards for statistical power and elicitation effort; no shared, cross-organisation standard exists yet.
nodes.entry_points: UK AISI is the clearest named home for this theme and periodically hires into it; the science-of-evaluations questions otherwise surface as a sub-topic inside METR's, Epoch AI's or Apollo Research's own methodology write-ups rather than as a standalone programme to join.

nodes.name: Benchmarks and evaluation tooling
nodes.definition: Shared benchmarks, task environments and software platforms used across the field to run evaluations and compare models' capabilities and safety-relevant behaviour, including autonomy and long-horizon task suites, and the engineering needed to host and run them at scale.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without shared, current benchmarks and harnesses, every evaluator rebuilds its own, results cannot be compared, and fast capability gains outrun measurement.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Maintained, openly available benchmarks and evaluation harnesses that any organisation can run quickly against a new model, staying ahead of saturation.

canonical_reference.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

key_agendas.name: Inspect evaluation framework and Inspect Evals
METR time-horizon benchmarks
Epoch AI benchmarking hub
Humanity's Last Exam (CAIS and Scale AI)

nodes.boundary_notes: Owns the benchmark and the harness. Datasets and training environments built to advance safety research generally, rather than to measure models, are meta.tooling.shared-research-infrastructure; benchmarks for interpretability methods are model.interpretability.interpretability-benchmarks; projecting trends from benchmark results is meta.evidence.capability-forecasting.
nodes.capacity_note: UK AISI and Meridian Labs maintain Inspect, and METR, Epoch AI, CAIS and MLCommons maintain widely used benchmarks, which fast capability gains keep saturating.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Open benchmarks and harnesses (METR's time-horizon suite, Epoch's FrontierMath) are updated periodically as saturation approaches.
nodes.entry_points: The Inspect Evals repository accepts community-contributed benchmarks and is the quickest way to get an evaluation used across the field. METR and Epoch AI hire and publish open problems; Andon Labs is a smaller group for anyone wanting to build a novel agentic environment rather than extend an existing benchmark.

nodes.name: Sandbagging and capability elicitation
nodes.definition: Testing whether a model can deliberately underperform on evaluations to hide dangerous capabilities or intentions, including 'evaluation awareness', where a model recognises it is being tested and behaves differently, and developing elicitation techniques (better prompting, fine-tuning, tool access) that reveal a model's true capability ceiling despite this.
nodes.why_it_matters: If a model can sandbag convincingly, every dangerous-capability evaluation is unreliable exactly when it matters most, since a model motivated to hide a capability is the scenario the evaluation was meant to catch.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Elicitation protocols with a demonstrated ability to unmask deliberately hidden capabilities, becoming a standard, mandatory step before any evaluation is reported as a clean result.

canonical_reference.title: AI Sandbagging: Language Models can Strategically Underperform on Evaluations

key_agendas.name: Stress-testing capability elicitation with password-locked models (Redwood Research)
Sabotage evaluations for frontier models (Anthropic)
Evaluation awareness research (Apollo Research)

nodes.boundary_notes: Measurement and counter-measurement of hidden capability. Why a model might sandbag is model.alignment.scheming; general evaluation rigour is model.evaluations.science-of-evaluations.
nodes.capacity_note: Carried mainly by Apollo Research, with Redwood Research, Anthropic and METR contributing elicitation methods and Poseidon Research working on detecting concealment.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Elicitation techniques such as targeted fine-tuning and improved prompting are used ad hoc by evaluators; no mandatory, standardised anti-sandbagging step exists before an evaluation is reported.
nodes.entry_points: Apollo Research publishes open problems and hires directly into this line of work, the clearest route in; the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy's synthesis report on evaluation awareness is a good way to see the state of the evidence before diving into primary research.

subareas.name: Model security
subareas.definition: Protecting the AI system itself, its weights, training and deployment infrastructure, agents, supply chain and the people with access to it, from theft, tampering, sabotage and exploitation. This is security work with the model as the asset being protected, not the model as a weapon.
subareas.scope_rule: In: defending the model, its weights, infrastructure, agents, supply chain and privileged people against attackers and insiders. Out: AI used as a weapon against other targets (misuse.cyber); government rules on chips and compute (society.compute-governance); pipelines for security talent (meta.talent.senior-and-specialist-recruitment).

nodes.name: Weights and infrastructure security
nodes.definition: Preventing theft, unauthorised exfiltration or tampering of frontier model weights and the compute, storage and network infrastructure that trains and serves them, commonly graded using RAND's SL1-5 security levels.
nodes.why_it_matters: Stolen weights give the thief the model's full capability with whatever safeguards they choose to strip out, and an attacker only has to succeed once. That makes weight security one of the highest-leverage single points of failure in the field.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Leading labs operating at RAND's higher security levels (SL4-5) as a matter of course, verified by independent security capacity, not just self-reported.

canonical_reference.title: Securing AI Model Weights: Preventing Theft and Misuse of Frontier Models

key_agendas.name: RAND SL1-5 security levels
Tailwind: Security capacity buildout
Achieving AI Model Weight Security Level 3 (SL3)

nodes.boundary_notes: Classical security applied to protecting the model. AI as the attacker's tool is misuse.cyber; the hiring pipeline for nation-state-grade security staff is meta.talent.senior-and-specialist-recruitment; tampering during training rather than theft of finished weights is model.model-security.supply-chain-and-integrity; threats from people with legitimate access are model.model-security.insider-threat. Copying a model's capabilities by distilling its API outputs, rather than stealing its weights, is a related threat not yet covered by a separate node.
nodes.capacity_note: RAND's security levels now have capacity-building behind them (IST's SL5 Task Force and the Security Level 5 nonprofit's draft standard), while actual lab practice remains self-reported.
nodes.existing_mitigations: RAND SL1-5 grading; the SL5 Standard (60 controls/12 families); lab-internal ASL/preparedness-framework security tiers.
nodes.entry_points: The IST SL5 Task Force and the Security Level 5 nonprofit are actively building out technical working groups (machine, network, software, supply chain, personnel security) and are the clearest open, non-lab route in; RAND publishes its research openly and hires for its emerging-risk teams. This is a genuinely under-supplied niche for someone with classical security or cloud infrastructure experience rather than ML research experience.

nodes.name: Agent and application security
nodes.definition: Security specific to LLM-powered applications and autonomous agents: prompt injection, tool-use exploitation, excessive agency granted to an agent, and insecure handling of model outputs that get executed or acted on downstream.
nodes.why_it_matters: As agents are given real tool access (browsing, code execution, payments), a successful prompt injection or exploited tool call can cause real-world harm directly, not just a bad chat response.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Agent designs that give real guarantees against prompt injection, for example by keeping untrusted data from ever steering which actions an agent takes (as in Google DeepMind's CaMeL design), alongside a mature shared standard for agentic applications. Unlike classic web vulnerabilities, prompt injection has no known complete fix at the model level, so progress is as much architectural as a matter of hygiene.

canonical_reference.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026

key_agendas.name: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
OWASP Agentic Security Initiative
CaMeL: defeating prompt injections by design (Google DeepMind)
AgentDojo prompt-injection benchmark (ETH Zurich)

nodes.boundary_notes: Defends an agent assumed to be aligned from outside manipulation, most often prompt injection. Restricting an agent because it may itself be misaligned is model.control.agent-sandboxing; adversarial prompts aimed at extracting prohibited content from the model itself are model.model-security.jailbreak-robustness.
nodes.capacity_note: A large commercial market that consolidated quickly in 2025 and 2026 through acquisitions, alongside the OWASP standards effort; the research problem of robust defence against prompt injection has far fewer people on it.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Commercial guardrail/agent-firewall products; OWASP Top 10 for LLM/Agentic Applications; open-source red-teaming tools (Promptfoo).
nodes.entry_points: OWASP's GenAI Security Project and Agentic Security Initiative are open to collaborators and the best non-commercial way in. Promptfoo's open-source project takes contributions (OpenAI announced its acquisition in 2026). AgentDojo and similar open benchmarks are a good starting point for research on prompt-injection defences. Most other named organisations are commercial vendors, several now inside large security companies.

nodes.name: Supply chain and model integrity
nodes.definition: Keeping the data, software and hardware that go into a model free of tampering (poisoned data, inserted backdoors, compromised dependencies), and being able to verify afterwards that a deployed model is the one intended and has not been secretly modified.
nodes.why_it_matters: A poisoned or backdoored model can pass ordinary testing and then behave harmfully on a trigger, and without integrity checks no one, including the developer, can tell.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Chain-of-custody controls for training data and code, and standard integrity attestations that let a developer, auditor or regulator confirm a model's provenance, as ordinary practice at frontier developers.

canonical_reference.title: A small number of samples can poison LLMs of any size (Anthropic, UK AISI and Alan Turing Institute, 2025)

key_agendas.name: Tailwind: AI integrity standards
OpenSSF model signing (Sigstore model-transparency)
Sleeper Agents: backdoors that persist through safety training

nodes.boundary_notes: The integrity of the model itself. Verifying that states or developers are keeping an agreement about compute or training runs is society.compute-governance.agreement-verification, which may use similar attestation techniques; theft of finished weights is model.model-security.weights-security; insiders deliberately planting hidden loyalties is model.model-security.insider-threat.
nodes.capacity_note: Commercial vendors scan models and dependencies and the OpenSSF model-signing work covers basic provenance, but no organisation focuses on provenance and poisoning defence for frontier-scale training.
nodes.owner_field: software supply-chain security (OpenSSF, Sigstore, SLSA) and commercial ML security vendors
nodes.connection_note: Model signing and scanning are maturing in the supply-chain community, but nobody yet provides chain of custody for a frontier model's training data and process strong enough for an auditor to rely on, which needs supply-chain security people working with AI safety evaluators.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Commercial ML model/pipeline scanning (HiddenLayer, Protect AI/Prisma AIRS); general security consultancy audits (Trail of Bits); MITRE ATLAS threat cataloguing.
nodes.entry_points: No AI-safety-native organisation owns training-data chain-of-custody or model-provenance attestation specifically, which the Tailwind fund names as a live gap; this is a genuinely open niche for someone with supply-chain security or cryptographic attestation background. The commercial scanning vendors (HiddenLayer, Trail of Bits) are hiring and a more accessible adjacent entry point.

nodes.name: Insider threat
nodes.definition: Treating employees, contractors and other insiders with privileged access to model weights, training infrastructure or deployment systems as a security surface: access controls, anomaly detection, audit logging, vetting, and preventing a small group from covertly steering a model toward their own interests.
nodes.why_it_matters: As frontier AI becomes more strategically and commercially valuable, a single insider with sufficient access can exfiltrate weights, sabotage safety measures, or covertly bias a model's behaviour without any external attacker involved.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Insider-threat programmes at frontier labs comparable in rigour to those in national-security or nuclear contexts, including technical controls that make it detectable if a small group tries to alter a model's behaviour without broader sign-off.

canonical_reference.title: We Need to Talk About the Insider Risk from AI

key_agendas.name: Tailwind: Investigations for secret loyalties
AI-enabled coups: how a small group could use AI to seize power (Forethought)
How personnel security can inform AI insider risk

nodes.boundary_notes: Assumes the humans with access may be untrustworthy, whereas model.control assumes the model may be; an AI agent with privileged access acting as an insider is model.control. Detecting a planted backdoor after the fact overlaps model.model-security.supply-chain-and-integrity; the wider question of a small group using AI to seize power is society.structural-risk.concentration-of-power.
nodes.capacity_note: IST's SL5 Task Force runs a personnel-security workstream and Anthropic makes public insider-threat commitments, but no independent organisation works mainly on insider threat at AI developers.
nodes.existing_mitigations: IST SL5 personnel-security workstream; lab-internal compartmentalization and access-restriction commitments (e.g. Anthropic RSP).
nodes.entry_points: IST's SL5 Task Force personnel-security working group is the clearest concrete route in for someone with classical personnel-security or counter-insider-threat background applied to AI labs. Coefficient Giving's 'Investigations for secret loyalties' Tailwind initiative is an explicit, funded-adjacent open question with no named org yet running point.

nodes.name: Jailbreaks and adversarial robustness
nodes.definition: Defending a deployed model against adversarial inputs, whether handcrafted, optimised, or discovered via automated search, designed to elicit outputs the developer intended to prohibit.
nodes.why_it_matters: A safety mitigation that a motivated user can bypass with a clever prompt provides no real protection once the model is generally available; robustness against this kind of attack is what makes safety training meaningful in deployment.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Defences that hold up against adaptive attackers who know the defence exists and are optimising specifically to beat it, not just against the fixed set of jailbreaks used to build the defence.

canonical_reference.title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail? (Wei, Haghtalab and Steinhardt, 2023)

Constitutional Classifiers (Anthropic)
HarmBench standardised red-teaming evaluation (CAIS)
The attacker moves second: adaptive attacks break published defences
MITRE ATLAS adversarial ML tactics and techniques

nodes.boundary_notes: Resisting deliberate adversarial prompts against a trained model. The wider safeguards system around a deployed model (classifiers, monitoring, enforcement) is model.developer-assurance.deployment-misuse-safeguards; how training makes values generalise is model.alignment.robust-generalisation; attacks on the agents and applications built around a model, such as prompt injection, are model.model-security.agent-security; stripping safeguards by modifying open weights is misuse.open-weights.safeguard-removal.
nodes.capacity_note: A well-funded commercial red-teaming and guardrail market with many overlapping vendors, plus lab safeguards teams and academic research; defences that hold against adaptive attackers remain an open research problem with fewer people on it.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Commercial automated red-teaming platforms; guardrail/classifier models; MITRE ATLAS threat cataloguing.
nodes.entry_points: Promptfoo's open-source project and public jailbreak arenas (Gray Swan) are the two most person-agnostic routes in, needing no application process. The genuinely open problem, defences that hold against an adaptive attacker who knows the defence, is an academic research gap rather than a product gap; most named orgs compete on the product side of a now-crowded market.

subareas.name: Reliability and failures
subareas.definition: AI systems causing harm through ordinary failure, with no bad actor and no misaligned goal: agents whose errors compound, confident false statements, and malfunctions of AI embedded in critical and safety-critical systems. Google DeepMind's safety approach calls this risk family mistakes and the International AI Safety Report calls it reliability; it is where AI safety meets classical safety engineering.
subareas.scope_rule: In: unintended failures of AI systems doing what they were asked, their consequences in critical systems, and methods for assuring AI in safety-critical products. Out: models pursuing goals their developers did not intend (model.alignment); attacks on or with AI (model.model-security and the Harmful use layer); measuring capabilities (model.evaluations).

nodes.name: Agent reliability and error propagation
nodes.definition: AI agents that carry out long, multi-step tasks fail in ways single answers do not: a small early mistake compounds over dozens of steps, agents misread instructions or tool outputs, loop, give up or wrongly declare success, and systems of several agents pass errors between them. An agent can succeed at a task one time and fail unpredictably the next, and success rates fall as tasks get longer and the required reliability rises.
nodes.why_it_matters: As agents are given real permissions over code, money and infrastructure, an agent that is right most of the time but fails unpredictably can do serious damage with no bad actor and no misaligned goal involved.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Agent evaluations that report consistency and failure modes rather than only average success, agent designs that detect and recover from their own errors, and deployment practice that matches an agent's permissions to its measured reliability.

canonical_reference.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., 2025)

key_agendas.name: Holistic Agent Leaderboard reliability dashboard (Princeton)
Measuring AI ability to complete long tasks (METR time horizons)
MAST taxonomy of multi-agent system failures

nodes.boundary_notes: Unintended failures of agents doing what they were asked. An agent pursuing goals its developers did not intend is model.alignment; an agent manipulated by an outside attacker is model.model-security.agent-security; containing an untrusted agent is model.control.agent-sandboxing; measuring how long a task an agent can complete is model.evaluations.benchmarks-and-tooling; interactions between independently operated agents are society.structural-risk.multi-agent-risk.
nodes.capacity_note: Public measurement comes from a few academic and nonprofit efforts (Princeton's Holistic Agent Leaderboard, METR's time horizons, failure taxonomies such as MAST), while companies building agents do reliability engineering in-house and publish little.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Human approval steps for consequential actions, limited permissions, and retries and checks built into agent frameworks; most public benchmarks still report average success rather than consistency.
nodes.entry_points: Princeton's HAL harness and METR's task suites are open and can be run on public models, and reproducing a failure analysis such as MAST on a new agent system is a practical first project. Companies that deploy agents hire reliability and evaluation engineers.

nodes.name: Hallucination and factual errors
nodes.definition: Language models state false information fluently and with confidence: invented facts, citations, legal cases, software packages or medical details. OpenAI's 2025 analysis argues that standard training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, so the problem persists as models improve. It is distinct from dishonesty, where a model states something it has reason to believe is false.
nodes.why_it_matters: People increasingly act on model outputs in law, medicine, finance and software without checking them, so confident errors cause real harm and erode trust even when nobody intends any.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Models that are calibrated about what they know and abstain when unsure, evaluations that reward that behaviour rather than guessing, and measured error rates that users and deployers can rely on in high-stakes settings.

canonical_reference.title: Why Language Models Hallucinate (Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang, OpenAI, 2025)

key_agendas.name: Evaluations that reward abstention over guessing (OpenAI)

nodes.boundary_notes: Unintended false statements. A model knowingly stating falsehoods is a question of honesty, measured in model.evaluations.propensity-and-character-evals; errors compounding across a multi-step task are model.reliability.agent-reliability; the consequences in critical systems are model.reliability.high-stakes-deployment-failures.
nodes.capacity_note: A large academic literature on factuality, commercial detection tools and leaderboards (Vectara) and developers' own work on calibration and abstention, though it is rarely framed as a safety problem.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Retrieval from trusted sources, citation checking, commercial and open hallucination-detection models, and human review in regulated uses; none removes the underlying incentive to guess.
nodes.entry_points: Hallucination and factuality are active academic research topics with open benchmarks, and Vectara's leaderboard and detection model are open source. Developers' post-training and evaluation teams work on calibration and abstention.

nodes.name: AI failures in critical systems
nodes.definition: AI embedded in systems where failure is costly (energy grids and industrial control, healthcare, finance, transport) creates new ways for those systems to fail with no attacker involved: models that behave unpredictably outside the conditions they were built for, give operators confident but wrong advice, or add hard-to-audit dependencies to systems that must stay up. Guidance for operators on integrating AI safely is only beginning to appear.
nodes.why_it_matters: In critical systems a single malfunction can cascade into physical harm, outages or financial loss, and the safety arguments these sectors rely on were not written for components that learn from data and behave statistically.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Sector-specific guidance and testing that operators actually apply before AI goes into critical systems, incident reporting that distinguishes AI failures, and reliable fallback to safe manual operation when an AI component misbehaves.

key_agendas.name: CISA, NSA and partners: principles for secure integration of AI in operational technology

nodes.boundary_notes: Failures of AI inside critical systems with no attacker. AI-enabled attacks on the same systems are misuse.cyber.critical-infrastructure; formal assurance of AI in certified products such as vehicles and aircraft is model.reliability.safety-critical-assurance; unreliable agents in general are model.reliability.agent-reliability.
nodes.capacity_note: National cyber agencies have issued joint principles for integrating AI into operational technology, but sector-specific testing and incident data on AI failures in critical systems are still scarce.
nodes.owner_field: operators and regulators of critical sectors (energy, health, finance, transport) and their safety engineering practice
nodes.connection_note: Operators and regulators receive general guidance on integrating AI, but little flows from developers and safety researchers about how general-purpose models fail in operational use, or from operators back into developers' evaluations.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Sector regulation and engineering practice (redundancy, manual fallback, change control) limit what a single component failure can do, and the joint principles from CISA, NSA, NCSC and international partners give operators AI-specific guidance for operational technology.
nodes.entry_points: National cyber and infrastructure agencies such as CISA and NCSC publish guidance and hire. For AI safety researchers, testing how general-purpose models behave in operational settings, and sharing that with operators, is open ground.

nodes.name: Safety-critical AI assurance
nodes.definition: Showing, to the standard regulators require, that an AI component in a safety-critical product (a car, aircraft, medical device or railway system) is safe enough to certify. Established safety engineering relies on specified requirements, hazard analysis and exhaustive testing, which machine-learning components do not fit well, so the functional-safety community has been writing new guidance: ISO/PAS 8800 for AI in road vehicles, UL 4600 for autonomous products, EASA's guidance for machine learning in aviation, and assurance methods such as York's AMLAS.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without accepted methods for assuring learned components, either unsafe AI enters products that can kill people or useful AI is kept out, and frontier AI safety cases miss decades of practice from these fields.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Accepted assurance methods and standards for machine-learning components are applied in certification and extended to products built on general-purpose models, and frontier AI safety cases draw on the same practice.
