nodes.definition: Facial recognition and other AI identification and monitoring systems deployed at national or city scale to track people's movements and associations, including states using these tools to track and intimidate dissidents, journalists and diaspora communities abroad.
nodes.why_it_matters: It removes the practical limits that have constrained surveillance, making dissent and minority life far riskier, and now reaches across borders.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Enforceable legal limits on mass biometric surveillance in more jurisdictions, and host states able to detect and respond to AI-enabled targeting of diaspora communities.

canonical_reference.title: The Global Expansion of AI Surveillance (Carnegie Endowment for International Peace)

nodes.boundary_notes: The deployed surveillance practice. Suppressing speech is misuse.surveillance.censorship; scoring and predicting individuals is misuse.surveillance.predictive-policing-and-scoring; restricting sales of these tools abroad is misuse.surveillance.export-controls; how power becomes concentrated enough to enable this is society.structural-risk.concentration-of-power.
nodes.capacity_note: An established digital-rights and human-rights field documents AI surveillance deployments well, with the cross-border and diaspora strand thinner.
nodes.owner_field: digital rights and human rights
nodes.connection_note: Developers' threat reports now describe disrupting surveillance tooling and one developer's refusal of domestic mass surveillance became a legal fight in 2026; what should flow is developers' case data to rights researchers and rights groups' threat models into usage policies and monitoring.
nodes.existing_mitigations: The EU AI Act has prohibited, since February 2025, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion recognition at work and in schools, and real-time remote biometric identification in public by police except in narrow cases. Data-protection law (GDPR and equivalents), export controls on surveillance goods, and human-rights monitoring and litigation (Citizen Lab, Access Now, Amnesty) continue to apply. AI developers' usage policies are a new lever: the 2026 dispute in which the US Department of Defense labelled Anthropic a supply-chain risk turned partly on its refusal to allow domestic mass surveillance.
nodes.entry_points: Access Now's Digital Security Helpline and general AI programme are the most open route for a technically-minded entrant wanting to help targeted individuals directly. Citizen Lab runs fellowships and is based at a university, making it the clearest academic route in.

nodes.name: AI-enabled censorship
nodes.definition: AI systems used to detect, filter or suppress prohibited speech and content at national scale, including automated censorship built directly into widely-used AI products and services within a jurisdiction.
nodes.why_it_matters: AI dramatically lowers the cost of comprehensive, real-time content censorship compared to human review, letting a state monitor and suppress dissent across far more content and languages than manual censorship ever could.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Independent, regularly updated audits track which AI products censor what, in which jurisdictions, and this information is accessible to affected users rather than hidden.

canonical_reference.title: China's AI-Empowered Censorship: Strengths and Limitations (Carnegie Endowment)

nodes.boundary_notes: Suppressing content, where misuse.influence-operations.covert-campaigns pushes it; the same state may do both. Surveillance of people rather than content is misuse.surveillance.mass-surveillance.
nodes.capacity_note: Digital-rights censorship researchers (Citizen Lab, OONI, Freedom House, Carnegie) are extending their measurement to AI-based filtering, and CAISI has evaluated censorship built into open-weight models.
nodes.owner_field: digital rights
nodes.connection_note: The rights field and the evaluation community barely connect; evaluation methods for censorship inside models should flow into rights research, and rights groups' country knowledge into evaluators' prompts and benchmarks.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Circumvention tools (Tor, VPNs) and monitoring by digital-rights groups (Freedom House, Citizen Lab, OONI) were built against pre-AI censorship and are being extended, evidenced by Carnegie's and Freedom House's recent AI-specific output, rather than replaced.
nodes.entry_points: Citizen Lab's fellowship programme is the clearest academic route in for someone with a technical measurement background. Freedom House and Carnegie both take contributions to their annual reports from country experts and are approachable via their standard contact channels.

nodes.name: Predictive policing and social scoring
nodes.definition: AI systems used to predict criminal behaviour, allocate policing resources, or score individuals' trustworthiness or loyalty for access to services, employment or freedom of movement, often reproducing or amplifying existing discrimination.
nodes.why_it_matters: These systems can lock in and automate discrimination at a speed and scale no individual human decision-maker could match, while their predictive basis is often difficult for an affected person to see or challenge.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Predictive-policing and social-scoring systems are subject to mandatory bias auditing, an affected person can get a meaningful explanation and challenge a decision, and the clearly harmful uses are prohibited, as the EU AI Act now does for social scoring and for predicting individual offending based solely on profiling.

canonical_reference.title: Algorithmic Policing: When Predicting Means Presuming Guilty (AlgorithmWatch)

nodes.boundary_notes: State or powerful-actor use for social control. Unfair outcomes in otherwise legitimate commercial uses are society.ethics-fairness-welfare.fairness-and-bias; the literatures overlap heavily and some organisations will tag to both.
nodes.capacity_note: AlgorithmWatch, Fair Trials, Amnesty and similar organisations have tracked algorithmic policing and scoring for years and publish recent country case studies.
nodes.owner_field: digital rights and criminal-justice reform
nodes.connection_note: Most systems here come from specialist vendors rather than frontier developers, so little flows between the rights field and AI developers and little yet needs to; the link to watch is police use of general-purpose models.
nodes.existing_mitigations: The EU AI Act prohibits social scoring and individual crime prediction based solely on profiling (from February 2025) and classes other law-enforcement uses as high-risk. Anti-discrimination and due-process law, and audit and litigation by AlgorithmWatch, Fair Trials, Amnesty and others, apply whether or not the tools use modern AI.
nodes.entry_points: AlgorithmWatch explicitly welcomes outside contributors and collaborators for its country case studies. Fair Trials' predictive-policing campaign page is the clearest legal/advocacy route in for someone with a criminal-justice background.

nodes.name: Surveillance technology export controls
nodes.definition: Restricting the sale and transfer of AI-powered surveillance systems (facial recognition, network monitoring, predictive policing software) from companies in democracies to states that would use them for repression.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without export controls, the technical capability built for legitimate uses in one country becomes directly available for repression in another, effectively laundering responsibility for the harm through a commercial transaction.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Export-control regimes for AI-enabled surveillance technology are as developed and enforced as existing controls on conventional dual-use and military technology, with verified end-use monitoring.

canonical_reference.title: Regulating transfers of AI algorithms, training data and models: The potential and limitations of export controls (SIPRI)

key_agendas.name: SIPRI Dual-Use and Arms Trade Control programme on AI transfers
EU Dual-Use Regulation 2021/821 (cyber-surveillance catch-all)

nodes.boundary_notes: Trade controls on surveillance systems and software. Controls on AI chips are society.compute-governance.export-controls; the deployed practice is misuse.surveillance.mass-surveillance.
nodes.capacity_note: Dual-use export-control policy (SIPRI, the Wassenaar process, the EU dual-use regulation) exists but has no settled category for AI surveillance software.
nodes.owner_field: export control and dual-use trade policy
nodes.connection_note: Technical input on how to define and verify a controllable category of AI surveillance system, of the kind compute governance has developed for chips, should flow from AI safety into export-control policy, and currently does not.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Existing dual-use export-control regimes (the Wassenaar Arrangement, the EU dual-use regulation's cyber-surveillance catch-all clause, national export-control lists) already cover conventional surveillance hardware and are being adapted, slowly and without settled norms, to AI-specific software and models.
nodes.entry_points: SIPRI's Dual-Use and Arms Trade Control Programme is the clearest specialist route in and publishes openly on exactly this gap. Privacy International works with outside collaborators and technologists through its broader surveillance-industry research.

subareas.name: Open-weight models
subareas.definition: Models whose weights are published, which is a release choice rather than a harm domain. Open weights let anyone inspect, adapt and run a model, bringing research, defensive and competition benefits, and they also mean safety training can be cheaply stripped (by fine-tuning or abliteration) and uncensored variants can spread. The harms themselves land in the other sub-areas of this layer; this sub-area holds what is specific to open release.
subareas.scope_rule: In: stripping safeguards from models whose weights are available, the supply of the resulting uncensored models (including criminal services), and independent assessment of the marginal risk and benefit of open release. Out: the developer's own release-decision process (model.developer-assurance.frontier-safety-frameworks); techniques that make safeguards resist removal (model.alignment.unlearning-and-tamper-resistance).

nodes.name: Safeguard removal from open weights
nodes.definition: Removing refusal behaviour and safety training from a model whose weights are available, either by cheap fine-tuning on a small dataset or by directly editing weights or activations to delete the refusal direction ('abliteration'), which needs no training data and is a widely shared recipe.
nodes.why_it_matters: If safeguards can be removed in minutes, any open-weight model should be treated as having none, which changes what it is safe to release.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Reliable measurements of how cheaply each kind of safeguard is removed, used in release decisions, and defences that raise that cost substantially.

canonical_reference.title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To! (Qi et al., 2023)

key_agendas.name: Refusal is mediated by a single direction (Arditi et al., 2024), the basis of abliteration
Tamper-resistant safeguards (TAR; Tamirisa et al., 2024)
Abliteration-resistant tuning (Kuo, Yadav and Smith, 2026)

nodes.boundary_notes: The attack side. Making safeguards survive fine-tuning is model.alignment.unlearning-and-tamper-resistance; the interpretability understanding that abliteration exploits is model.interpretability.safety-applications; distribution of the resulting models is misuse.open-weights.uncensored-model-supply.
nodes.capacity_note: Mostly academic papers on abliteration, one commercial vendor (Alice) publishing measurement research, and UK AISI's worst-case testing under adversarial fine-tuning.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Model licences and terms of service formally prohibit safeguard removal, though this is largely unenforceable once weights are public; there is no other non-AI-native mitigation for this specific technique.
nodes.entry_points: Alice publishes its abliteration research openly and is the clearest industry contact point; independent replication of the arXiv papers (2605.26526 and 2607.17427) on new model families is a low-barrier way for a new researcher to add evidence, since coverage of specific model families is thin.

nodes.name: Uncensored model supply
nodes.definition: The hosting, packaging and sale of models whose safeguards have been removed, from uploads on mainstream model-hosting platforms to underground services (sometimes branded, such as 'WormGPT'-style offerings) that sell uncensored models for writing malware, phishing and scam scripts.
nodes.why_it_matters: Distribution decides whether a stripped model stays a research curiosity or reaches a broad population of would-be criminals.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Ongoing tracking of how uncensored models spread and are sold, and hosting and payment chokepoints that make large-scale criminal services harder to run.

canonical_reference.title: Malla: Demystifying Real-world Large Language Model Integrated Malicious Services (USENIX Security 2024)

nodes.boundary_notes: Distribution and retail. Stripping the safeguards is misuse.open-weights.safeguard-removal; the fraud and cyber harms that follow are misuse.fraud-and-abuse.fraud-and-impersonation and misuse.cyber.offensive-uplift.
nodes.capacity_note: Security vendors (Alice, Trend Micro, Cisco Talos) track the uncensored-model marketplace, but nobody works to disrupt its distribution or payment chokepoints.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Hosting platforms' content policies, app-store rules and payment processors' terms are the main levers, and they work when applied: payment-processor pressure led at least one large model-sharing site (Civitai) to restrict real-person likeness models in 2025. Criminal services moved to self-hosting and crypto payments in response.
nodes.entry_points: Threat-intelligence teams at Alice, Trend Micro and Cisco Talos publish openly and are the most direct way to see current marketplace structure; there is no dedicated disruption-focused organisation to join, which is itself the gap an entrant could fill.

nodes.name: Open-weight release: marginal risk and benefit
nodes.definition: Frameworks and evidence for judging what a given open-weight release adds, in both risk and benefit, compared with models already available. On the risk side, safeguards can probably be removed after release and a release cannot be recalled; on the benefit side, open models let researchers, defenders and smaller companies and countries inspect, adapt and run models themselves, and spread capability beyond a few developers. After the July 2026 OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, open-model advocates argued that responders needed open models because closed-model safeguards had blocked their forensic work.
nodes.why_it_matters: Open-weight releases cannot be recalled, and blanket restriction would also give up research, defensive and competition benefits; credible independent assessment of marginal risk and benefit is what lets policymakers and developers decide release by release rather than by assumption.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Independent researchers, not only the releasing developer, produce credible assessments of marginal risk and benefit for major open-weight releases, and these assessments visibly inform release decisions, post-release mitigations and policy.

canonical_reference.title: On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models (Kapoor, Bommasani et al., ICML 2024)

key_agendas.name: NTIA report on dual-use foundation models with widely available weights (2024)
UK AISI open-weight risk management programme
CAISI evaluation of DeepSeek models (2025)

nodes.boundary_notes: Independent assessment of what an open-weight release adds, in risk and in benefit. The developer's own release process is model.developer-assurance.frontier-safety-frameworks; national rules on open release would be society.public-policy.legislation; concentration of capability in a few closed developers is society.structural-risk.concentration-of-power.
nodes.capacity_note: UK AISI runs an open-weight risk programme with EleutherAI and Oxford, US CAISI evaluated DeepSeek's models, Stanford CRFM set out the marginal-risk framework, and Hugging Face started an Open Alignment team in September 2026.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Dual-use research of concern (DURC) oversight frameworks from biosecurity are the closest pre-existing model, adapted by analogy, for gating the release of a dual-use artefact.

open_problems_source.title: Open Technical Problems in Open-Weight AI Model Risk Management

nodes.entry_points: UK AISI's open-weight work and EleutherAI are both openly collaborative and publish methodology; Hugging Face's new Open Alignment Team (announced September 2026) is the freshest and most likely to be actively hiring or seeking collaborators as it stands up.

layers.role_line: People and states using it to cause harm

layers.name: Society and Government
layers.definition: Structural risks that no single system or actor causes, and the governance of AI by governments and international bodies: law, standards, diplomacy, compute controls, economic transition, the information ecosystem, and ethics, fairness and welfare.

subareas.name: Structural risk
subareas.definition: Harms that arise from the interaction of many actors, companies, states and AI systems, where no single system is misaligned and no single actor is misusing AI, but the aggregate effect erodes safety, competition or human control. Covers competitive dynamics between developers and states, concentration of power, multi-agent interactions, and slow shifts in who or what holds effective societal control.
subareas.scope_rule: In: risks from aggregate incentives and interactions across many actors or systems (racing, power concentration, multi-agent dynamics, gradual loss of human influence and oversight, strategic stability). Out: one developer's safety practice (model.developer-assurance) and deliberate weaponisation by a bad actor (misuse layer).

nodes.name: Race dynamics
nodes.definition: Competitive pressure between AI companies, and between states, to develop and deploy more capable systems faster than safety work can keep pace, including cutting corners on testing to avoid losing ground to rivals.
nodes.why_it_matters: Racing is a collective-action trap: each developer or state may privately prefer more caution but cannot afford to slow down alone, so testing is cut short and the chance rises that a dangerous system ships before anyone has checked it properly. Many other problems on this map, from evaluations to international agreements, get harder under racing pressure.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Credible mechanisms, such as verified agreements or coordinated pacing, that let competitors slow down together without any one of them losing decisive ground, backed by monitoring that would expose defection.

canonical_reference.title: An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks (Hendrycks & Woodside), section on the AI race

key_agendas.name: Superintelligence Strategy and its deterrence framing, Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang, 2025)
Forethought's research on navigating a fast or discontinuous transition
Convergence Analysis's US-China race scenarios and ASI treaty framework

nodes.boundary_notes: The incentive problem. The machinery that might solve it is society.international-governance.treaties and society.compute-governance.agreement-verification; one lab's own commitments are model.developer-assurance.frontier-safety-frameworks.
nodes.capacity_note: Think tanks (Forethought, Convergence Analysis, CAIS, the AI Futures Project) describe the racing dynamic and a few scenario and treaty proposals exist, but nobody works directly on changing the incentives.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Voluntary inter-lab coordination on safety practice through the Frontier Model Forum. Some published frontier safety policies now say the developer may relax its own requirements if a rival releases a comparable system without equivalent safeguards (for example OpenAI's April 2025 Preparedness Framework update), which writes racing pressure into policy rather than containing it. No verified mechanism for coordinated pacing exists between labs or states.

open_problems_source.title: AI-Enabled Coups (Forethought) and Toward ASI Stability (Convergence Analysis) both discuss racing incentives as a driver of other structural risks

nodes.entry_points: Forethought and Convergence Analysis both publish open research questions and take on researchers or fellows on transition and race-dynamics strategy; the Frontier Model Forum is closed to labs rather than open to individual entrants. There is no dedicated organisation working on race-slowing mechanisms themselves, so an entrant with a background in mechanism design, verification technology or game theory has genuinely open ground here.

nodes.name: Concentration of power
nodes.definition: The risk that advanced AI capability, and the economic and political power that flows from it, becomes concentrated in a very small number of companies, states or individuals, potentially letting a small group seize or entrench outsized control.
nodes.why_it_matters: A small group could use AI-enabled surveillance, persuasion or economic dominance to escape the checks and balances that normally constrain power, whether by seizing it outright or by quietly dominating the markets everyone else depends on.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Mechanisms for distributing AI capability and its governance, such as broad deployment norms, oversight bodies with real authority, and checks on any single actor's control of decisive AI infrastructure, in place before capability becomes decisive.

canonical_reference.title: AI-Enabled Coups: How a Small Group Could Use AI to Seize Power (Tom Davidson, Lukas Finnveden & Rose Hadshar, Forethought, April 2025)

key_agendas.name: Forethought's power-concentration and AI-enabled coups research
AI Now Institute's research on corporate and state power concentration
The Intelligence Curse (Drago and Laine, 2025), on what happens to states and citizens when labour stops being a source of power
UK Competition and Markets Authority review of AI foundation models

nodes.boundary_notes: A specific group gaining outsized control, whether by seizing political power or by dominating the markets for compute, cloud and frontier models. The two strands have different communities (AI-risk strategy on seizure of power; competition law and political economy on market concentration) and an entrant should know both exist. Everyone losing influence with no beneficiary is society.structural-risk.gradual-disempowerment; a state that already holds power using AI for repression is misuse.surveillance; insiders secretly steering a model is model.model-security.insider-threat.
nodes.capacity_note: Forethought works on the mechanics of seizing power and the AI Now Institute on corporate and economic concentration, with nobody yet building countermeasures full time.
nodes.existing_mitigations: None in force; the Forethought report itself proposes candidate mitigations (e.g. transparency about military and intelligence use of AI, checks on exclusive model access) that have not yet been adopted by any government or lab.
nodes.entry_points: Forethought publishes open research questions from the AI-enabled coups report and is a natural first stop for anyone wanting to work on countermeasures (transparency mechanisms, checks on military/intelligence AI use, distributed oversight). AI Now Institute is hiring and publishes on corporate power concentration for those more interested in the economic and antitrust angle.

nodes.name: Gradual disempowerment
nodes.definition: The risk that humans progressively lose effective influence over economic, cultural and political systems as AI performs more of the functions those systems depend on, including the loss of any human or institution's timely ability to review, override or halt what the aggregate system is doing, even when each deployment passes its own review and no one intends the outcome.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents a slow, hard-to-notice slide into irrelevance for human judgement and preferences across institutions, a failure mode that classic loss-of-control framings centred on a single rogue AI can miss entirely.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Institutions that can demonstrate they still track and act on human preferences as AI automates more of their internal functions, plus early-warning indicators for when that stops being true.

canonical_reference.title: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development (Kulveit, Douglas, Ammann, Turan, Krueger & Duvenaud, 2025)

key_agendas.name: Gradual Disempowerment research agenda and position paper
AI Objectives Institute's work on collective alignment as a countermeasure
UK AISI's societal resilience research theme

nodes.boundary_notes: Can occur even if every system is aligned to its operator (contrast model.alignment) and with no specific beneficiary (contrast society.structural-risk.concentration-of-power). Oversight of a single deployment is model.control.control-protocols.
nodes.capacity_note: ACS Research treats gradual disempowerment as a standing research programme, with the AI Objectives Institute working nearby.
nodes.existing_mitigations: None in force; the paper and ACS Research's follow-on agenda propose research directions (measuring disempowerment, hierarchical-agency frameworks, oversight indicators) rather than deployed mitigations.
nodes.entry_points: ACS Research's own site lists open research questions and hiring; the gradual-disempowerment.ai site lists a concrete research-projects post on the Alignment Forum that names specific tractable sub-questions an entrant could pick up. AI Objectives Institute also takes on researchers for its collective-alignment and deliberation-tool work.

nodes.name: Multi-agent risks
nodes.definition: Risks and open problems arising from interactions between multiple AI systems, such as unstable equilibria, collusion, negotiation failure, or conflict escalation between AI agents acting on behalf of different principals.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents harms that no single system's designer would predict from testing it in isolation, including AI-driven conflicts that could be more severe or harder to de-escalate than purely human ones.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Tested protocols and institutions for AI-to-AI interaction, such as negotiation, commitment devices, and verification, that keep multi-agent systems in cooperative rather than adversarial equilibria, validated in realistic simulated environments before wide deployment.

canonical_reference.title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI (Hammond et al., Cooperative AI Foundation technical report, 2025)

key_agendas.name: Cooperative AI Foundation's research agenda
Center on Long-Term Risk's work on reducing risks of AI conflict (s-risks)

nodes.boundary_notes: Interactions between independently operated AI systems. One organisation controlling one untrusted model is model.control.control-protocols; deliberate weaponisation is misuse.military.
nodes.capacity_note: A dedicated funder (Cooperative AI Foundation), a research institute (CLR), a startup betting on multi-agent alignment (Softmax) and Google DeepMind's benchmark infrastructure, still a small share of safety effort.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Benchmark suites (Melting Pot) and a growing academic literature on multi-agent reinforcement learning safety; no deployed institutional mechanism yet for AI-to-AI negotiation or verification in real-world settings.
nodes.entry_points: The Cooperative AI Foundation runs grants, workshops (including a NeurIPS workshop series) and is the most person-agnostic route in; CLR runs a named fellowship; Softmax is hiring directly for its research agenda. Google DeepMind's Melting Pot is open source and usable by anyone wanting to build or test multi-agent evaluation methods without needing to join a lab.

nodes.name: AI and strategic stability
nodes.definition: How the spread of advanced AI affects the risk of war or crisis escalation between states, including faster decision cycles, new opportunities for miscalculation, and pressure to integrate AI into nuclear or conventional command and control.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents AI from making great-power crises more likely to spiral into war by compressing decision time, degrading mutual understanding of intentions, or creating incentives for pre-emption.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Confidence-building measures and crisis-communication channels adapted for an AI-saturated environment, plus clear norms, such as keeping humans in nuclear command decisions, adopted by the major military powers.

canonical_reference.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Strategic Stability and Nuclear Risk, Volume I (SIPRI, 2019)

key_agendas.name: SIPRI's programme on AI and strategic stability
CNAS's AI and national security work
Superintelligence Strategy's deterrence proposal (MAIM), and the debate it started about stability between AI powers

nodes.boundary_notes: Crisis escalation and command-and-control effects of military AI adoption. Weapons that select targets are misuse.military.lethal-autonomy and misuse.military.decision-support; the diplomatic channels are society.international-governance.great-power-dialogue.
nodes.capacity_note: Arms-control and strategic-studies institutions (SIPRI, CNAS, RAND) run AI-specific programmes on nuclear risk, escalation and command and control.
nodes.owner_field: arms control and strategic studies
nodes.connection_note: The research is strong, but little of it reaches AI developers and AI governance bodies as shared standards or channels, and developers' knowledge of what their models can do in military settings rarely flows back.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Longstanding nuclear confidence-building and crisis-communication channels (hotlines, notification regimes) that predate AI, now under study for how they need to adapt. Non-binding statements exist: the US and China affirmed in November 2024 that humans, not AI, should control decisions to use nuclear weapons; the US-led Political Declaration on Responsible Military Use of AI and Autonomy (2023) and the REAIM summits set broader norms. No binding AI-specific agreement among the major military powers exists.

open_problems_source.title: SIPRI's programme on AI and strategic stability

nodes.entry_points: SIPRI and CNAS both publish open research and hire from national-security and technical backgrounds; RAND runs fellowships and is a large, standard entry point into this field for those with a policy or technical-security background. This is not a node where an AI-safety-native newcomer organisation is obviously missing; the more useful route in for an entrant is through these existing institutions.

subareas.name: Public policy and regulation
subareas.definition: The domestic law-making, regulators, standards and administrative capacity through which governments oversee AI development and deployment, including who is liable for AI-caused harm, how safety-relevant information reaches regulators and the public, and the rules and shared infrastructure for AI agents.
subareas.scope_rule: In: making national and subnational law, regulators and enforcement, liability, standards and their adoption, whistleblower law, a state's technical capacity, and rules and public infrastructure for AI agents. Out: the assurance mechanisms a law may require, such as frontier safety frameworks, safety cases, audits and incident reporting, which stay in model.developer-assurance whether voluntary or mandated; agreements between states (society.international-governance); campaigning for policy (meta.communications.advocacy).

nodes.name: Domestic AI legislation
nodes.definition: Statutes and regulations passed by national or subnational governments that impose binding requirements on the development or deployment of AI systems, such as the EU AI Act or US state-level frontier AI safety laws.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents reliance on companies' voluntary commitments alone by giving legal force and enforcement teeth to safety and transparency requirements.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A small number of well-designed, interoperable statutes, rather than a patchwork of conflicting rules, that are actually enforced, cover frontier-scale risk without strangling beneficial uses, and are updated as capabilities change.

canonical_reference.title: EU AI Act regulatory framework overview (European Commission)

key_agendas.name: EU AI Act implementation: general-purpose AI obligations in force since August 2025, the GPAI Code of Practice (July 2025), and the Digital Omnibus deferral of high-risk obligations to December 2027 (agreed May 2026)
US state frontier AI statutes: California SB 53 (2025), New York RAISE Act (2025), Illinois SB 315 AI Safety Measures Act (2026)
US federal pre-emption push: December 2025 executive order creating an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws
Secure AI Project's state-by-state tracking of frontier AI bills

nodes.boundary_notes: Making and passing binding law within one jurisdiction, and the regulators and enforcement that follow. The assurance mechanisms a law requires (frontier safety frameworks, incident reporting, audits, safety cases) sit in model.developer-assurance whether voluntary or mandated; co-regulatory codes such as the EU GPAI Code of Practice are part of the law-making here, while the frameworks they ask for are model.developer-assurance.frontier-safety-frameworks; cross-border agreements are society.international-governance.treaties; campaigns for legislation are meta.communications.advocacy.
nodes.capacity_note: Advocacy organisations, legal researchers and legislatures work on AI statutes, and binding frontier-model law now exists in the EU, California, New York and Illinois, amid US federal efforts to pre-empt state laws.
nodes.entry_points: Encode and Secure AI Project both take volunteers and welcome contact from people who want to work on state or federal AI bills, and LawAI publishes open legal research questions. CLTR's expert-placement programme (see regulatory-capacity) is a route into UK government policy work specifically.

nodes.name: Liability for AI harms
nodes.definition: Legal frameworks that determine who is responsible, and who must pay, when an AI system causes harm, including questions of developer versus deployer liability and how existing tort and product-liability law applies to AI.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents a situation where victims of AI-caused harm have no effective legal remedy and where developers face no financial incentive to invest in safety because liability is unclear or unenforceable.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Clear, tested liability rules, whether through new statute or judicial interpretation of existing law, that assign responsibility in a way that incentivises safety investment without making beneficial deployment commercially impossible.

canonical_reference.title: U.S. Tort Liability for Large-Scale Artificial Intelligence Damages: A Primer for Developers and Policymakers (RAND, 2024)

key_agendas.name: EU revised Product Liability Directive (2024/2853), which brings software and AI systems within strict product liability for products placed on the market from 9 December 2026
Institute for Law & AI's liability research
Test cases in US courts over chatbot harms, such as Garcia v. Character Technologies and Raine v. OpenAI
EU's withdrawn AI Liability Directive and its aftermath

nodes.boundary_notes: Who pays and who is at fault. Statute more broadly is society.public-policy.legislation; responsibility for harm caused by AI agents specifically is society.public-policy.agent-accountability; a developer's internal risk arguments are model.developer-assurance.safety-cases.
nodes.capacity_note: LawAI is the one specialist nonprofit doing sustained AI liability research, with RAND and academic tort scholars contributing while courts hear the first chatbot-harm cases.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Ordinary tort, negligence and product-liability law; the EU's revised Product Liability Directive from December 2026; early US court decisions on whether chatbot output is a product or protected speech.
nodes.entry_points: LawAI is effectively the only dedicated route in; it publishes open research questions on AI liability and is small enough that direct outreach is realistic for someone with a legal research background.

nodes.name: Accountability and liability for agent actions
nodes.definition: Who is responsible when an AI agent acting on someone's behalf causes harm: the developer of the model, the company that deployed the agent, the user who instructed it, or nobody. Existing law assumes a person or company takes each consequential action; agents that sign up to services, move money or run code blur that, and proposals range from applying agency law to requiring agents to follow the law by design.
nodes.why_it_matters: If nobody is clearly accountable for what agents do, harms go uncompensated, the incentive to deploy agents carefully weakens, and courts and legislators settle the question case by case after the damage.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A clear allocation of responsibility among developers, deployers and users for agent actions, tested in law or regulation, and agents designed to follow the law and leave the records that accountability needs.

canonical_reference.title: Governing AI Agents (Noam Kolt, Notre Dame Law Review, 2025)

key_agendas.name: Law-Following AI: designing AI agents to obey human laws (Institute for Law & AI)

nodes.boundary_notes: Responsibility for harm caused by agents specifically. Liability for AI harms in general is society.public-policy.liability; identifying and tracing agents is society.public-policy.agent-infrastructure; building agents that do not pursue unintended goals is model.alignment.
nodes.capacity_note: Legal scholarship on governing agents (Kolt) and LawAI's work on law-following AI set out the questions, but no organisation focuses on responsibility for agent actions and no jurisdiction has settled it.
nodes.existing_mitigations: General tort, contract, product-liability and agency law apply, and the revised EU Product Liability Directive brings AI software under strict liability for products placed on the market from December 2026; none of it was written with autonomous agents in mind.
nodes.entry_points: The Institute for Law & AI publishes on law-following AI and runs a workshop series on it; legal scholars working on agency law and product liability can contribute directly. Developers' terms of service for agent products are where responsibility is allocated in practice today.

nodes.name: Standards and certification
nodes.definition: Technical standards and conformity-assessment frameworks written specifically for AI safety and security, covering management-system standards such as ISO/IEC 42001, risk-management frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its 2024 Generative AI Profile, the harmonised standards being drafted under the EU AI Act, frontier-model evaluation and red-teaming standards, and the safety and security work inside IEEE and CEN-CENELEC. Covers how these standards are written and how they get adopted, whether voluntarily by developers or written into law and procurement.
nodes.why_it_matters: Standards turn general safety principles into checkable, AI-specific requirements; weak or paperwork-only standards give false assurance, and laws that lean on them inherit their gaps.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Standards specific enough to frontier AI risks that certification means something, with independent verification of substantive rather than paper compliance.

canonical_reference.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)

key_agendas.name: NIST AI RMF (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage), under revision following the July 2025 US AI Action Plan
NIST Generative AI Profile
ISO/IEC 42001
EU AI Act harmonised standards (CEN-CENELEC JTC 21)
ETSI baseline cyber security requirements for AI systems (EN 304 223)
IEEE AI standards (e.g. IEEE 7000 series)

nodes.boundary_notes: One node for AI-specific standards whoever adopts them. Scope rule: in scope only for standards written for AI safety, security, risk-management or evaluation purposes; out of scope are generic IT service-management, information-security or quality standards not specific to AI (for example ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 27001), even where an AI company happens to hold that certification. A developer's own frameworks are model.developer-assurance.frontier-safety-frameworks; content-provenance standards are society.epistemics.content-provenance; model integrity standards are model.model-security.supply-chain-and-integrity.
nodes.capacity_note: NIST, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42, CEN-CENELEC JTC 21, IEEE, the AI Verify Foundation, AI Standards Lab and MLCommons all produce AI-specific standards; uptake by frontier developers and independent verification of compliance lag behind.
nodes.entry_points: MLCommons and AI Verify Foundation both explicitly invite outside contributors to their open frameworks, and AI Standards Lab is small enough for direct contact. The formal standards bodies (NIST, ISO, CEN-CENELEC, IEEE) work through public comment periods and technical committee membership rather than informal entry.

nodes.name: Whistleblower protection
nodes.definition: Legal and organisational mechanisms that let employees or contractors at AI companies safely report safety-relevant concerns, near-misses or violations, including protection from retaliation and channels for right-to-warn disclosures.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents safety-relevant information from staying trapped inside a company because employees fear losing their job, equity, or facing legal action for speaking up.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Statutory protections, not just company policy, covering AI-sector employees specifically, tested in practice by real cases, plus safe and credible external channels that a whistleblower can actually use.

canonical_reference.title: How to Design AI Whistleblower Legislation (Institute for Law & AI)

key_agendas.name: California's frontier AI whistleblower protections (SB 53, 2025)
EU AI Act Article 87: the EU Whistleblower Directive applies to AI Act breaches
Connecticut SB 5 and Illinois SB 315 (2026)
Proposed US federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act

nodes.boundary_notes: Legal protection created and enforced by government. Practical legal, financial and reputational support from outside organisations is meta.watchdogs.whistleblower-support; internal channels are model.developer-assurance.internal-safety-governance.
nodes.capacity_note: Statutory protection now exists in California, Connecticut, Illinois and the EU but is untested, and only a handful of organisations work on the law itself.
nodes.entry_points: LawAI (legal design), the National Whistleblower Center (federal campaign and support for individuals) and the AI Whistleblower Initiative (policy advocacy alongside its support work) are all small enough to contact directly. Anyone with employment-law experience can usefully track how the new state and EU protections are being used.

nodes.name: Government technical capacity
nodes.definition: The technical staff, compute, tools and institutional knowledge a government needs to understand frontier AI, test it and act on what it finds. That might sit in a regulator with enforcement powers (such as the EU AI Office) or in a non-regulatory technical institute that advises ministers and tests models by agreement (such as the UK AI Security Institute or the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation). This is separate from the text of the law itself.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents a situation where good laws exist on paper but regulators lack the technical expertise or resources to tell whether a company is actually complying, letting enforcement become theatre.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Regulatory bodies with in-house technical staff able to run their own evaluations, interpret companies' safety claims critically, and keep pace with the state of the art, comparable to how financial regulators employ their own quants.

canonical_reference.title: Regulating AI in the UK (Ada Lovelace Institute, 2023)

key_agendas.name: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) capacity-building
UK AISI's pre-deployment evaluation capacity

nodes.boundary_notes: Technical capacity inside one government. Coordination between national institutes is society.international-governance.institutions; the independent auditors a regulator might rely on are model.developer-assurance.third-party-auditing; public grant funding for independent research is meta.funding.funding-concentration.
nodes.capacity_note: The EU AI Office, UK AISI, US CAISI and a network of national institutes give some governments real technical capacity, while most governments, sector regulators and US states have little.
nodes.entry_points: UK AISI and CAISI both post job openings for technical staff evaluating frontier models. CLTR runs an expert-placement route into UK government for people with a relevant policy or technical background.

nodes.name: Agent identity, visibility and protocols
nodes.definition: The shared infrastructure that would let people, companies and governments know which AI agents are acting, on whose behalf and with what permissions: identifiers and authentication for agents, logs and disclosure of agent activity, and the protocols agents use to call tools and talk to each other. Most of this is being built now by companies and standards bodies, and whether it supports accountability depends on choices made early.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without identity and visibility, harms caused by agents cannot be traced, rules for agents cannot be enforced, and an incident involving many agents cannot be reconstructed or stopped.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Widely adopted open standards for agent identity and authorisation, activity records that incident investigators and regulators can use, and protocols that carry accountability information by default.

canonical_reference.title: Infrastructure for AI Agents (Chan et al., 2025)

key_agendas.name: AI Agent Standards Initiative (NIST Center for AI Standards and Innovation, February 2026)
IDs for AI Systems (GovAI)
The 2025 AI Agent Index: technical and safety features of deployed agents

nodes.boundary_notes: Rules and shared infrastructure for identifying and tracing agents across developers and deployers. Securing a particular agent against attack is model.model-security.agent-security; who is liable when an agent causes harm is society.public-policy.agent-accountability; standards for AI in general are society.public-policy.standards; interactions between agents as a systemic risk are society.structural-risk.multi-agent-risk.
nodes.capacity_note: NIST launched an AI Agent Standards Initiative in February 2026 and GovAI publishes the core research on agent IDs and visibility, while the protocols themselves are being built by companies with little accountability design.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Early standards work, including NIST's AI Agent Standards Initiative (launched February 2026, with a workstream on agent identity and authorisation), industry protocols for tool use and agent-to-agent communication, and research proposals for agent IDs and activity logs; no identity scheme is yet widely adopted.
nodes.entry_points: NIST's initiative has sought public input, and GovAI publishes the core research. Engineers working on agent protocols and authentication in industry are building the infrastructure itself, and proposing accountability features there is open ground.

subareas.name: International governance
subareas.definition: The treaties, multilateral institutions and diplomatic processes through which states coordinate on AI risk across borders, including great-power dialogue and who gets a voice.
subareas.scope_rule: In: treaties, multilateral institutions (including the network of AI safety institutes), great-power diplomacy and track-two dialogue, and inclusive participation. Out: one country's law (society.public-policy); verification technology (society.compute-governance.agreement-verification); weapons-specific arms control (misuse.military.lethal-autonomy).

nodes.name: International agreements
nodes.definition: Proposed and existing multilateral agreements that set shared rules for AI. The only binding treaty so far is the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (2024), which covers human rights, democracy and the rule of law, not frontier-model risk. It has been signed by the US, UK and EU and ratified by the EU. Everything aimed at frontier risk is non-binding (summit commitments) or proposed (red lines, draft treaties limiting frontier development).
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents a situation where safety measures adopted by one country are undercut by another country's more permissive rules, recreating race dynamics at the international level.
nodes.progress_looks_like: At least one substantive, verifiable agreement among the states that host frontier AI development, with real consequences for non-compliance, rather than a non-binding communique.

canonical_reference.title: International AI Institutions: A Literature Review of Models, Examples, and Proposals (Maas and Villalobos, LawAI, 2023)

key_agendas.name: The summit series: Bletchley AI Safety Summit 2023, Seoul 2024, Paris AI Action Summit 2025, India AI Impact Summit 2026
Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS 225)
Global Call for AI Red Lines (launched at the UN General Assembly, September 2025)
MIRI Technical Governance Team's draft international agreement to prevent premature superintelligence (2025)
ControlAI's campaign for a binding international agreement

nodes.boundary_notes: Negotiating and keeping agreements between states. Checking compliance is society.compute-governance.agreement-verification; the incentive problem is society.structural-risk.race-dynamics; unilateral company commitments are model.developer-assurance.frontier-safety-frameworks.
nodes.capacity_note: Advocacy and research on red lines and draft treaties has grown (AI Red Lines, MIRI, ControlAI, The Future Society, CeSIA), but government treaty-making on frontier risk has not started.
nodes.entry_points: ControlAI and The Future Society both campaign and research openly for binding international agreements and take on volunteers and researchers; this is one of the more advocacy-shaped, less technical entry points in the map.

nodes.name: International institutions
nodes.definition: Standing multilateral bodies that convene governments, and sometimes industry and civil society, on AI on an ongoing basis. Examples are the OECD (which now hosts the Global Partnership on AI), the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and Global Dialogue on AI Governance, and the network of national AI safety and security institutes, renamed the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science, through which national institutes coordinate testing methods.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without standing venues, coordination depends on one-off summits and technical findings stay national.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Institutions with clear mandates and enough technical capacity to produce joint outputs, such as shared evaluation methods, that members actually adopt.

canonical_reference.title: Governing AI for Humanity: final report of the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI

key_agendas.name: OECD.AI Policy Observatory, OECD AI Principles and the integrated Global Partnership on AI
UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance (established August 2025)
International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (formerly the International Network of AI Safety Institutes)
G7 Hiroshima AI Process reporting framework, run by the OECD

nodes.boundary_notes: The standing bodies. Capacity inside any one government is society.public-policy.regulatory-capacity; who gets a seat is society.international-governance.inclusive-participation; the evaluations institutes run are model.evaluations.dangerous-capability-evals.
nodes.capacity_note: The OECD, the UN's Scientific Panel and Global Dialogue, and the renamed network of national institutes meet regularly and produce joint outputs; whether members adopt them is the open question.
nodes.entry_points: OECD.AI and the UN Scientific Panel are government-run and not open to informal outside contribution; WEF's AI Governance Alliance is comparatively more open to non-governmental participants, and the Simon Institute (see inclusive-participation) is the more realistic non-governmental route into this space generally.

nodes.name: US-China and cross-bloc dialogue
nodes.definition: Official and unofficial channels between the states most central to frontier AI, above all the United States and China, covering competition (export controls, chip restrictions) and cooperation (safety dialogues, crisis communication), including track-two dialogue between researchers and policy communities where government channels are thin.
nodes.why_it_matters: Any serious limit on dangerous AI development needs the leading powers to trust each other enough to agree and verify; without channels, misunderstandings escalate.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Durable government-to-government safety dialogue backed by sustained researcher-level exchanges that survive political shocks, extended to other country pairs.

canonical_reference.title: A Path Forward on AI Safety for the United States and China (Carnegie Endowment, 2026)

key_agendas.name: Concordia AI's bridging research and State of AI Safety in China report
IDAIS consensus statements from the International Dialogues on AI Safety (Safe AI Forum)
Proposed US-China AI safety notification channel between Treasury Secretary Bessent and Vice Premier He Lifeng (September 2026)

nodes.boundary_notes: The relationship and dialogue. The instrument of chip controls is society.compute-governance.export-controls; the military crisis risk is society.structural-risk.strategic-stability; formal treaty negotiation is society.international-governance.treaties.
nodes.capacity_note: Track-1.5 and track-2 dialogues (IDAIS, Concordia AI, Carnegie) continue and US-China government talks in September 2026 discussed a notification mechanism, with other country pairs thinly served.
nodes.entry_points: Concordia AI publishes an open, English-language State of AI Safety in China report and welcomes outside researchers; Safe AI Forum's IDAIS series is the most direct route into being part of a future dialogue.

nodes.name: Inclusive participation in global governance
nodes.definition: Efforts to ensure that countries outside the small group hosting frontier AI development, especially in the Global South, can meaningfully participate in shaping international AI governance rather than having rules set without them.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents international AI governance from being written by and for a handful of wealthy states, which risks rules that ignore other countries' interests and undermines the legitimacy and durability of any agreement reached.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Diplomats and technical experts from a broad range of countries actively shaping, not just receiving briefings on, major international AI governance processes, backed by their own domestic technical capacity.

canonical_reference.title: Governing AI for Humanity, final report of the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI (2024), especially its finding that 118 countries were party to none of the major non-UN AI governance initiatives

key_agendas.name: Simon Institute's diplomatic capacity-building programme
UN AI Advisory Body's attention to global representation
Global Index on Responsible AI (Global Center on AI Governance)

nodes.boundary_notes: Who gets a real voice in society.international-governance.institutions. Cyber defensive capacity in the same countries is misuse.cyber.defensive-capacity-gaps; local safety communities are meta.convenings.regional-hubs.
nodes.capacity_note: A few dedicated organisations (Simon Institute, ILINA, the Global Center on AI Governance) serve a widely acknowledged need, with growing interest from larger think tanks.
nodes.entry_points: Simon Institute runs fellowships placing people into Geneva-based diplomatic capacity-building; ILINA runs an African-led AI safety and policy talent programme. Both are realistic entry points for non-technical contributors.

subareas.name: Compute governance
subareas.definition: Using control over the physical and logistical chain behind AI computing hardware, chips, data centres and cloud access, as a lever to enforce AI policy, including export restrictions and mechanisms to verify how compute is actually used.
subareas.scope_rule: In: policy and technical mechanisms that govern who can access compute and for what, including export rules, diversion tracking, cloud reporting, and hardware-enabled verification of agreements. Out: securing a developer's own compute and weights (model.model-security); providing compute to safety researchers (meta.tooling.shared-research-infrastructure).

nodes.name: Chip export controls and diversion
nodes.definition: Government restrictions on selling advanced AI chips and chip-making equipment to specific countries or entities, and the technical and administrative means of tracking where chips end up so that smuggling and diversion around the rules can be detected.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents states of concern from rapidly closing the compute gap with leading AI developers, one of the few concrete levers governments currently have over the pace of frontier AI development elsewhere.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Export rules that are well-targeted, restricting genuinely risk-relevant compute without needlessly harming unrelated trade, consistently enforced across allied countries, and hard to circumvent through smuggling or shell entities.

canonical_reference.title: Computing Power and the Governance of Artificial Intelligence (Sastry, Heim et al., 2024)

key_agendas.name: US Bureau of Industry and Security's AI chip export rules
CSET's compute and export-control policy analysis
CNAS's AI chip supply chain security work

nodes.boundary_notes: The rule and its enforcement. Verifying what chips are computing, for agreements, is society.compute-governance.agreement-verification; the wider US-China relationship is society.international-governance.great-power-dialogue; export controls on surveillance tools are misuse.surveillance.export-controls.
nodes.capacity_note: CSET, CSIS, IAPS, CNAS, RAND and Epoch AI analyse rule design, chokepoints and diversion and BIS enforces, while the policy itself has swung back and forth since 2025.

open_problems_source.title: IAPS compute governance research (tag page, updated continuously)

nodes.entry_points: IAPS publishes the most open, hands-on compute-governance research agenda; Epoch AI is hiring and publishes open problems in compute forecasting and diversion tracking.

nodes.name: Verifying AI agreements
nodes.definition: The technical mechanisms and protocols that let one party check that a state or developer is complying with an agreement about AI development: hardware features in chips, such as secure enclaves and cryptographic attestation, that report how much compute was used and for what, plus the inspection and protocol design that would make such evidence usable between rivals, by analogy with nuclear arms-control verification.
nodes.why_it_matters: Agreements that cannot be verified are unlikely to be made between rivals, and unlikely to hold if made.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Chips shipping with agreed, privacy-preserving verification features and a tested protocol that two rival states could actually use.

canonical_reference.title: What Does It Take to Catch a Chinchilla? Verifying Rules on Large-Scale Neural Network Training via Compute Monitoring (Shavit, 2023)

key_agendas.name: IAPS compute governance and verification research
CNAS's hardware-enabled mechanisms and on-chip governance framework
Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG) design reports
MIRI Technical Governance Team's work on verifying international agreements
Hardware-Level Governance of AI Compute feasibility taxonomy

nodes.boundary_notes: Verification for governance. Integrity checks on a single model are model.model-security.supply-chain-and-integrity; the agreements themselves are society.international-governance.treaties; tracking where chips physically go for export enforcement is society.compute-governance.export-controls.
nodes.capacity_note: Research momentum grew through 2026 with several substantive papers and a small open-source hardware project (FlexHEG), though nothing is fielded.

open_problems_source.title: Near-Term Verification Methods for AI Chip Exports (Avellar and Grunewald, arXiv, September 2026)

nodes.entry_points: FlexHEG is an open-source community that takes outside contributors directly; IAPS publishes a full open compute-governance research agenda and is often hiring. This is one of the more tractable technical entry points in compute governance for someone with a hardware or cryptography background.

nodes.name: Cloud compute know-your-customer
nodes.definition: Know-your-customer obligations and usage-reporting requirements placed on cloud infrastructure providers, so that governments can see who is renting large amounts of AI-relevant compute and for what.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents actors from bypassing chip export controls entirely by renting compute in the cloud from a provider based in an unrestricted jurisdiction.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Cloud providers reliably identifying and reporting large training runs and high-risk customers to relevant regulators, implemented in a way that is technically enforceable and does not simply push activity to non-compliant providers.

canonical_reference.title: Oversight for Frontier AI through a Know-Your-Customer Scheme for Compute Providers (Egan and Heim, 2023)

key_agendas.name: US BIS proposed IaaS know-your-customer rule
IAPS compute governance research on threshold-based reporting

nodes.boundary_notes: Rented access to compute that never crosses a border as a physical good. Hardware sales are society.compute-governance.export-controls.
nodes.capacity_note: IAPS and GovAI researchers have done most of the design work, with the US know-your-customer rule for cloud providers still unfinalised.
nodes.entry_points: IAPS is the clearest entry point, publishing openly on this exact gap and generally open to outside researchers.

subareas.name: Economic transition
subareas.definition: How rapid AI-driven automation reshapes labour markets and the distribution of economic gains, and what policy responses could smooth that transition or share its benefits more broadly.
subareas.scope_rule: In: labour-market effects of AI and their timing, how the economic gains are shared, and how income support adapts. Out: unfair treatment of individuals by AI systems (society.ethics-fairness-welfare.fairness-and-bias); field-wide capability forecasting (meta.evidence.capability-forecasting).

nodes.name: Labour market disruption
nodes.definition: The disruption to jobs, wages and skill demand as AI automates tasks, and research modelling how fast and unevenly this could happen, so that policymakers get lead time rather than reacting after the fact.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents a transition that is fast enough, or concentrated enough in specific sectors and regions, to cause serious social and political instability before adaptation mechanisms such as retraining or safety nets can catch up.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Reliable, early data on which jobs and sectors are actually being automated and how fast, feeding into retraining and social-support programmes that are ready before mass displacement rather than after.

canonical_reference.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 2025)

key_agendas.name: Stanford Digital Economy Lab's AI Economic Indicators
Anthropic Economic Index
OECD AI and Work programme and Employment Outlook

nodes.boundary_notes: Who loses work and how fast. Who captures the gains is society.economic-transition.sharing-gains; how income support adapts is society.economic-transition.safety-nets; general capability timelines are meta.evidence.capability-forecasting.
nodes.capacity_note: Labour economists (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, MIT, Brookings, the OECD, the IMF) track AI's effects on work in close to real time, helped by developers' usage data.
nodes.owner_field: labour economics
nodes.connection_note: Developers now publish occupation-level usage data (Anthropic's Economic Index) that economists use and economists' analyses reach labs' policy teams; what flows less is AI safety's fast-scenario thinking into mainstream labour forecasts.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Real-time measurement infrastructure now exists (Stanford's dashboards, Anthropic's index) that did not a year ago; substantive policy mitigations (retraining pipelines, portable benefits) remain mostly proposals rather than adopted programmes, per Brookings' and Windfall Trust's own framing.

open_problems_source.title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning (Brookings/PIIE)

nodes.entry_points: Stanford Digital Economy Lab and the Anthropic Economic Index both publish open data and methodology that a researcher can build on without an insider connection; Epoch AI is hiring for forecasting work including GATE; Brookings and OECD publish open calls for policy fellows. This node has moved from thin to genuinely well-populated in the last twelve months.

nodes.name: Sharing the gains from AI
nodes.definition: Proposed mechanisms, such as windfall clauses, sovereign wealth-style funds, or new tax instruments, for ensuring the economic gains from transformative AI are shared broadly rather than captured almost entirely by a small number of AI developers and investors.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents extreme wealth concentration from advanced AI, which could itself become a driver of the power-concentration and social-instability risks covered elsewhere in this layer.
nodes.progress_looks_like: At least one credible, tested mechanism, such as a windfall clause signed by a major lab or a state-level sovereign fund tied to AI-driven growth, actually in force before the bulk of AI-driven gains materialise, rather than proposed only after the fact.

canonical_reference.title: The Windfall Clause: Distributing the Benefits of AI for the Common Good (O'Keefe et al., GovAI)

key_agendas.name: Windfall Trust's Windfall Policy Atlas
OpenAI's 2025 recapitalisation, which gave the nonprofit OpenAI Foundation a large equity stake in the for-profit company, as a live test of developer-side benefit sharing

nodes.boundary_notes: What happens to the surplus AI generates. Job loss itself is society.economic-transition.labour-disruption; conventional welfare machinery is society.economic-transition.safety-nets; power that flows from the same concentration of gains is society.structural-risk.concentration-of-power.
nodes.capacity_note: Essentially one dedicated organisation (Windfall Trust) plus GovAI's original proposal, with no mechanism yet adopted by a developer or government.
nodes.existing_mitigations: No windfall clause has been adopted. Partial precedents exist but were not designed for broad sharing: the OpenAI Foundation's equity stake after the October 2025 recapitalisation, and US government equity and revenue-share arrangements with chip firms in 2025. The Windfall Policy Atlas remains a catalogue of mostly unadopted options.
nodes.entry_points: Windfall Trust accepts contact through its site and publishes open research; it is effectively the single organisation to approach for anyone wanting to work on this problem specifically, alongside Forethought for the wider macrostrategy angle.

nodes.name: Adapting safety nets
nodes.definition: How existing welfare, healthcare, retraining and income-support systems need to change to remain functional if AI causes faster or larger-scale economic disruption than they were designed to handle.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents a gap opening between when displacement happens and when support systems, built for a slower and more localised pace of technological change, catch up, which is when the sharpest social harm occurs.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Pilot programmes and policy proposals, such as portable benefits, faster retraining pipelines, and contingency funding triggers tied to measurable displacement indicators, tested and ready to scale before a crisis rather than designed reactively.

canonical_reference.title: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work (IMF Staff Discussion Note, 2024)

key_agendas.name: Windfall Trust's broader policy-option catalogue

nodes.boundary_notes: The welfare-state machinery that must flex regardless of where the money comes from. Capturing and redirecting the surplus is society.economic-transition.sharing-gains.
nodes.capacity_note: Welfare economists and policy institutions study AI and work, and Windfall Trust covers safety-net redesign as one strand, but almost nobody designs for fast, economy-wide disruption.
nodes.owner_field: social policy and welfare economics
nodes.connection_note: Fast-scenario assumptions from AI safety, and indicators of displacement from developers' usage data, should flow into mainstream welfare design, which still assumes adoption spread over many years.
nodes.existing_mitigations: No AI-disruption-specific safety-net redesign has been adopted anywhere; existing welfare systems remain built for slower, more localised technological change.
nodes.entry_points: Windfall Trust is the most direct entry point given its dedicated policy-option catalogue; Brookings publishes fellowships and open workforce-policy research for those coming from a more conventional social-policy background.

subareas.name: Epistemics and information
subareas.definition: How AI reshapes society's ability to reason well, agree on facts and make good decisions together, including infrastructure and tools that could help (content provenance, deliberation platforms, decision support) and structural risks that could hurt.
subareas.scope_rule: In: structural effects of AI on collective reasoning, trust in information and decision-making, and the tools and infrastructure that could help, including content provenance and deepfake detection. Out: a specific actor deliberately manipulating an audience (misuse.influence-operations).

nodes.name: AI and collective reasoning
nodes.definition: How the growing use of AI to summarise, filter and mediate information changes society's capacity to reason accurately and reach shared understanding, for better or worse.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents a slow degradation of society's ability to identify true claims and make sound collective decisions, which would undermine the basis for almost all other governance responses to AI risk.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Measurable evidence that AI-mediated information systems improve, rather than degrade, people's calibration and shared understanding of contested facts, tracked over time rather than assumed.

canonical_reference.title: How Will Advanced AI Systems Impact Democracy? (Summerfield et al., 2024)

key_agendas.name: AI Objectives Institute's work on AI for collective sense-making
Forecasting Research Institute's work on improving judgement quality

nodes.boundary_notes: The diagnostic question of what ordinary AI use does to shared reasoning. Deliberate manipulation is misuse.influence-operations; tools that actively help are society.epistemics.deliberation-tools and society.epistemics.decision-quality.
nodes.capacity_note: The AI Objectives Institute and Forecasting Research Institute research it, and deployed systems such as Community Notes and Full Fact are studied for their effects.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Community Notes and Full Fact's tools are deployed, evidence-backed interventions at meaningful scale, though neither was designed with AI-safety framing; both are best read as existing real-world evidence about whether AI-mediated systems can help rather than purpose-built safety interventions.
nodes.entry_points: AI Objectives Institute and Forecasting Research Institute both publish open research and take on researchers; Full Fact publishes technical detail on its claim-matching pipeline and is a plausible place to contribute for someone from an NLP or civic-tech background. Community Notes' bridging algorithm is open source (birdwatch/Community Notes GitHub), a low-friction way to study or extend a real deployed system without joining X.

nodes.name: Deliberation tools
nodes.definition: AI-assisted tools designed to help large groups of people deliberate, express nuanced views, and reach legitimate collective decisions, such as AI-mediated public consultation platforms.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents democratic and civic institutions from becoming purely reactive to AI-driven change, by giving them AI-assisted means to actually incorporate broad public input into fast-moving decisions.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Deliberation tools used by real governments or institutions at meaningful scale, with independent evidence that they improve, rather than merely simulate, legitimate collective decision-making.

canonical_reference.title: AI Can Help Humans Find Common Ground in Democratic Deliberation (Tessler et al., Science, 2024)

key_agendas.name: AI Objectives Institute's Talk to the City deliberation tool
Polis, the open-source deliberation platform (Computational Democracy Project)
Collective Intelligence Project's Global Dialogues and Alignment Assemblies

nodes.boundary_notes: Tools for publics and large groups to deliberate. Tools for specific high-stakes institutional decisions are society.epistemics.decision-quality; the diagnostic question is society.epistemics.collective-reasoning.
nodes.capacity_note: The AI Objectives Institute, the Collective Intelligence Project and the Computational Democracy Project run tools with real government and institutional use, with limited independent evidence that they improve decisions.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Polis has demonstrated adoption at national scale in Taiwan and reported use in the UK; Talk to the City and CIP's Global Dialogues have been used in specific consultation pilots; none yet has the kind of routine, large-scale institutional adoption the node's 'progress looks like' criterion describes.
nodes.entry_points: The Computational Democracy Project is open source (github.com/compdemocracy) and welcomes external contributors and researchers directly; the Collective Intelligence Project runs an annual research fellowship; AI Objectives Institute takes on researchers for Talk to the City. This is one of the more approachable nodes for a technically-minded entrant.

nodes.name: Content provenance and deepfake detection
nodes.definition: Standards and tools for marking AI-generated or manipulated content at creation (provenance, watermarking, authentication) and for detecting it afterwards, so that people and platforms can tell synthetic media from authentic recordings whatever the intent behind it.
nodes.why_it_matters: If authentic and synthetic media cannot be told apart, evidence, journalism and identity checks lose their value, and genuine recordings can be dismissed as fake.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Provenance widely adopted across capture devices, generators and platforms, and detection that keeps pace with the newest generators.

canonical_reference.title: Reducing Risks Posed by Synthetic Content: An Overview of Technical Approaches to Digital Content Transparency (NIST AI 100-4, 2024)

key_agendas.name: C2PA content provenance standard
EU AI Act Article 50 marking and disclosure duties (applying from August 2026) and the Commission's code of practice on labelling AI-generated content
China's measures for labelling AI-generated content (in force September 2025)
Google DeepMind's SynthID watermarking
Partnership on AI's guidance on synthetic media

nodes.boundary_notes: General-purpose infrastructure. Its use against covert campaigns is misuse.influence-operations.covert-campaigns and against fraud is misuse.fraud-and-abuse.fraud-and-impersonation; AI management standards are society.public-policy.standards.
nodes.capacity_note: An industry standards coalition (C2PA), Partnership on AI and a growing set of detection vendors work here, with uneven adoption and detection lagging the newest generators.
nodes.existing_mitigations: C2PA provenance metadata is now supported by some capture devices and generative tools; commercial detection tools such as GetReal Security's platform are deployed for fraud and impersonation defence; neither keeps pace fully with the newest generation models.
nodes.entry_points: C2PA's specification and working groups are open to join; GetReal Security is a commercial employer for anyone with a detection or biometrics background; Partnership on AI publishes open guidance documents anyone can build on.

nodes.name: Decision quality in key institutions
nodes.definition: Whether the governments, regulators, courts and company boards that will make the most consequential decisions about AI can reason well under uncertainty and resist being overwhelmed or manipulated, including purpose-built AI tools that help with specific high-stakes decisions.
nodes.why_it_matters: The most important decisions about AI will be made quickly by a small number of institutions; if their reasoning is poor, good evidence elsewhere is wasted.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Decision-makers routinely using well-tested forecasting and AI decision-support tools, with evidence that they improve decisions.

canonical_reference.title: AI Tools for Existential Security (Vaintrob and Cotton-Barratt, Forethought, 2025)

key_agendas.name: Effective Institutions Project's work on institutional capacity
Quantified Uncertainty Research Institute's tools for reasoning under uncertainty
AI for decision-makers (Tailwind initiative)

nodes.boundary_notes: The decision-makers and tools for them. Producing the evidence is meta.evidence; group deliberation by the public is society.epistemics.deliberation-tools.
nodes.capacity_note: The Effective Institutions Project and QURI work on it, with Metaculus's forecasting infrastructure nearby, but decision support for AI-related decisions is rarely anyone's named mandate.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Forecasting tournaments and probabilistic-reasoning tools exist and are used by some institutions on an ad hoc basis; no routine, institutionalised use of these tools by governments or regulators for AI-specific decisions was found.
