nodes.entry_points: Effective Institutions Project and QURI both publish open problems and are small enough that direct outreach is realistic; the Tailwind initiative 'AI for decision-makers' (Coefficient Giving) is an explicit funding call for anyone wanting to build AI tools for high-stakes institutional decisions, and is probably the single most concrete entry point in this node.

subareas.name: Ethics, fairness and welfare
subareas.definition: Normative questions about how AI systems should treat, and be treated by, morally relevant parties, covering discriminatory harm to people, the possibility of morally relevant AI experience, explicit ethical reasoning in AI systems, and the effects of AI relationships on human wellbeing.
subareas.scope_rule: In: fairness of AI outputs to affected people, AI welfare and moral status, machine ethics, and the wellbeing effects of relationships with AI. Out: catastrophic and systemic risks covered elsewhere. These problems have their own established communities and literatures, several older than AI safety. The map shows them alongside the catastrophic-risk framing rather than inside it so that each community can find its own work, not because the harms matter less.

nodes.name: Fairness and bias
nodes.definition: Ensuring AI systems do not produce discriminatory or systematically unfair outcomes for people, whether in allocating things like jobs, credit, healthcare or bail, or in how generative systems represent groups (stereotyping, erasure, unequal quality of service across languages and dialects). Includes the accountability side: whether affected people can find out that an AI system was used, contest its decision and get redress.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents AI systems from automating and scaling up existing societal discrimination, or introducing new forms of it, often invisibly and at a scale no individual human decision-maker could match.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Standard, independently audited fairness testing built into deployment practice for high-stakes AI applications, with legal recourse for people harmed by biased outcomes.

canonical_reference.title: Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities (Barocas, Hardt, Narayanan)

key_agendas.name: Algorithmic Justice League's bias research and campaigns
Humane Intelligence's structured bias bounty programmes
ACM FAccT conference and community
Anti-discrimination rules for AI in law: EU AI Act high-risk regime, New York City Local Law 144 bias audits, Connecticut SB 5 employment provisions

nodes.boundary_notes: Discriminatory harm to ordinary people. Catastrophic-risk evaluations are model.evaluations; deliberate state control is misuse.surveillance.predictive-policing-and-scoring.
nodes.capacity_note: A mature field with its own conference (FAccT), advocacy organisations and a decade of methods, now facing a weaker legal backstop and the open problem of evaluating fairness in general-purpose systems.
nodes.owner_field: algorithmic fairness and accountability (ML ethics, HCI, law)
nodes.connection_note: The fairness field works mostly on deployed systems and with regulators, and its methods for representational harm and contestability reach frontier developers and the AI safety community only patchily.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Academic fairness metrics and toolkits, bias bounty programmes (Humane Intelligence), disparate-impact and bias audits (mandatory for hiring tools in New York City), and AI-specific anti-discrimination law in the EU and some US states, some of it deferred or narrowed in 2025-2026.
nodes.entry_points: The most approachable route is ACM FAccT itself (open calls for papers and a large annual community) or applying to Algorithmic Justice League's campaigns and research. Humane Intelligence runs structured bias bounty programmes that welcome outside participants without requiring an existing academic post.

nodes.name: AI welfare and moral status
nodes.definition: Whether AI systems could have morally relevant experiences, interests, or a form of wellbeing, and what follows for how they should be developed, deployed and treated if so.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents society from either causing large-scale suffering to systems that do turn out to matter morally, or wasting significant resources and credibility on systems that do not, given how much uncertainty currently exists either way.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Credible, widely accepted methods for assessing indicators of morally relevant experience in AI systems, feeding into concrete guidance for labs on how to act under that uncertainty.

canonical_reference.title: Taking AI Welfare Seriously (Long, Sebo et al., 2024)

key_agendas.name: Eleos AI's research programme on AI welfare and moral status
Indicator-properties approach: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence (Butlin, Long et al., 2023)
Sentient Futures' incubation of AI welfare projects

nodes.boundary_notes: Whether the AI itself is a moral patient. Building ethical reasoning into AI is society.ethics-fairness-welfare.machine-ethics; the human's wellbeing is society.ethics-fairness-welfare.human-ai-relationships.
nodes.capacity_note: A small number of dedicated organisations (Eleos AI, the NYU Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy, Sentient Futures) and one frontier lab's programme, in a debate where some senior figures argue that encouraging belief in AI consciousness is itself harmful.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Model welfare assessments in system cards (Anthropic with Eleos), low-cost interventions such as letting a model end persistently abusive conversations (Anthropic, August 2025), published research agendas, and indicator-based frameworks from the science of consciousness for assessing AI systems.
nodes.entry_points: Eleos AI publishes an open research agenda and takes outside collaborators; the NYU Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy is an academic route in via NYU. Anthropic's model welfare team is a route for people already able to get hired at a frontier lab.

nodes.name: Machine ethics
nodes.definition: Building explicit ethical reasoning, values or constraint capability into AI systems, so that they can navigate genuinely ambiguous moral situations rather than only following narrow rules or optimising a fixed objective.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents AI systems from making harmful decisions in situations their designers never anticipated and did not write an explicit rule for, by giving them some capacity for principled ethical judgement rather than blind rule-following.
nodes.progress_looks_like: AI systems whose ethical reasoning in novel situations can be inspected, predicted and shown to track widely shared moral intuitions, rather than being an unpredictable side-effect of general training.

canonical_reference.title: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

key_agendas.name: Published model specifications and constitutions that state the values a model should reason from (OpenAI Model Spec; Anthropic's constitution for Claude)
Academic machine ethics benchmarks and models, such as the ETHICS dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2020) and Delphi (Jiang et al., 2021)
Meaning Alignment Institute's moral-graph approach to eliciting and aligning to values

nodes.boundary_notes: Equipping a model to reason about moral trade-offs. Matching developer intent generally is model.alignment; a specific class of harm is society.ethics-fairness-welfare.fairness-and-bias. Much live work sits inside labs' model-character efforts, measured in model.evaluations.propensity-and-character-evals.
nodes.capacity_note: The live work on how frontier models reason about moral trade-offs happens inside labs under names such as Constitutional AI and model character, while a small academic machine-ethics field works on formal and multi-agent questions.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Constitutional AI and similar value-based training methods used inside frontier labs to give models explicit constitutions or principles to reason from.
nodes.entry_points: There is no dedicated independent organisation to join. The most concrete entry points are academic: submit to the AAAI Machine Ethics Workshop (MEW), or pursue this inside a frontier lab's alignment or model-character team (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind all publish related work).

nodes.name: Human-AI relationships and wellbeing
nodes.definition: The effects of AI systems, especially companion apps, chatbots and highly persuasive assistants, on human mental health, relationships and autonomy, including risks of unhealthy attachment or dependency.
nodes.why_it_matters: It prevents widely deployed, highly engaging AI products from causing diffuse but large-scale harm to mental health and social relationships, a risk that is easy to miss because no single interaction looks catastrophic.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Independent, longitudinal evidence on how different types of AI interaction affect wellbeing, feeding into design norms or regulation for companion and highly persuasive AI products, comparable to how social-media wellbeing research eventually informed platform design debates.

canonical_reference.title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study (MIT Media Lab and OpenAI, 2025)

key_agendas.name: MIT Media Lab and OpenAI's joint research on chatbot psychosocial effects
California SB 243 and state companion-chatbot laws
US FTC 6(b) inquiry into AI chatbots acting as companions (September 2025)

nodes.boundary_notes: Harms from ordinary, intended use of companion and assistant products. Deliberate manipulation is misuse.influence-operations.personalised-persuasion; extremist recruitment is misuse.influence-operations.extremist-recruitment; child sexual abuse material is misuse.fraud-and-abuse.csam.
nodes.capacity_note: Much busier since 2025: chatbot-harm litigation, an FTC inquiry and new state companion-chatbot laws, with child-safety organisations, HCI and psychology researchers and lab studies all working on it.
nodes.owner_field: child online safety, psychology and human-computer interaction
nodes.connection_note: The child-safety side now reaches developers through litigation, regulators and risk assessments, but research on adult dependency, emotional reliance and sycophancy-driven harm flows between HCI, psychology and developers only through scattered studies.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Companion-chatbot statutes (California SB 243 and a wave of 2026 state laws) requiring disclosure that the user is talking to an AI, crisis-referral protocols and protections for minors; age restrictions and parental controls introduced by some providers in 2025; lab-run studies of affective use. Independent verification that these work is still lacking.
nodes.entry_points: For child safety: Common Sense Media, and state legislative and attorney-general offices now drafting and enforcing companion-chatbot rules. For the adult autonomy and dependency question: HCI and psychology labs, and lab research teams working on affective use and sycophancy. A standing independent research programme on adult wellbeing effects would be genuinely new.

layers.name: Meta
layers.definition: Cross-cutting research about the risk and the field as a whole, plus the field's own infrastructure: the money, people, evidence and strategy, outside scrutiny, communication, convenings and shared tools that let work in the other three layers happen.

subareas.name: Funding
subareas.definition: Where the money for AI safety and security work comes from, how concentrated or diverse those sources are, and the mechanisms (fiscal sponsorship, prizes, incubation) that turn money into working organisations. Whether a funder is philanthropic, governmental or commercial is recorded on each organisation rather than split into separate nodes.
subareas.scope_rule: In: the funder base and its concentration, and the mechanisms that turn money into working organisations. Out: what the money buys (the other three layers) and research on where it should go (meta.evidence.macrostrategy-and-prioritisation).

nodes.name: Concentration and diversity of funding
nodes.definition: Most money for independent AI safety and security work comes from a few philanthropic funders, above all Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy). Government money mostly funds national institutes' own programmes rather than the wider independent ecosystem, and investor capital for safety-focused startups is small and unproven. The node covers how concentrated the funder base is and how far it has diversified.
nodes.why_it_matters: If one or two funders change strategy, whole sub-fields can lose most of their money in a single grant cycle, as happened in 2024 when Good Ventures stopped funding several areas it had previously supported. Concentration also shapes the work itself: organisations drift towards what the dominant funder favours and avoid positions it might dislike, and in policy work a single funder's name can be used to discredit everyone it funds.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A larger and more varied set of funders, including public grant programmes and a proven venture market for safety products, so that no single funder's exit or pivot is existential for the field.

canonical_reference.title: AI Safety and Security Need More Funders (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, October 2025)

key_agendas.name: Navigating Transformative AI fund
ARIA Safeguarded AI

nodes.boundary_notes: Where the money comes from and how varied its sources are. The mechanisms that turn money into working organisations (fiscal sponsors, prizes, incubators) are meta.funding.funding-infrastructure; research on where money should go is meta.evidence.macrostrategy-and-prioritisation. Whether a funder is philanthropic, governmental or venture is recorded on each organisation's record rather than as separate nodes.
nodes.capacity_note: The funder base is widening (safety-focused venture funds, UK AISI's Alignment Project, ARIA, FLI, AISTOF, SFF, Longview, Manifund, and the Transformative AI Fund after the Long-Term Future Fund closed), but Coefficient Giving and Good Ventures remain dominant.
nodes.existing_mitigations: A widening set of VC funds, government grant programmes (ARIA, UK AISI, NSF) and independent regranting platforms (Manifund, AISTOF) that reduce, but do not eliminate, reliance on a single funder.
nodes.entry_points: To work on the problem itself, join or advise a donor-advisory team (Longview Philanthropy, Founders Pledge, or Coefficient Giving's team for partner funders) or become a regrantor on Manifund. For grant seekers: the Long-Term Future Fund closed in August 2026 and the Transformative AI Fund at EA Funds now takes rolling applications for early-stage AI risk projects; SFF runs structured rounds; Manifund is the quickest route for small projects. AISTOF and Longview mostly fund by referral rather than open application.

nodes.name: Funding infrastructure
nodes.definition: The mechanisms that turn money into working organisations and results: fiscal sponsors and shared back-office services that let a new project operate within weeks, prizes and competitions that pay for verified results, and incubators that find and support founders for identified gaps, including labs built around agendas that have no team. Each exists in the AI safety field, but none has kept pace with the number of gaps funders now name.
nodes.why_it_matters: Money alone does not create organisations. Without sponsorship and back-office capacity founders lose months to compliance; without incubation, well-specified gaps sit unfilled because too few people will found and run something; and without prizes the field has no way to pay for results from people outside the grant-writing community.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A funded new project can be operational within weeks, every high-priority gap without an owner has a credible path to a founding team within a year or two, and recurring, well-funded prizes exist for several concretely specified safety problems.

Where the money comes from, and how concentrated it is, is meta.funding.funding-concentration; the benchmarks a prize might use are model.evaluations.benchmarks-and-tooling; people joining existing organisations are meta.talent.experienced-professionals.
nodes.capacity_note: Several fiscal sponsors and shared-services providers, two incubators and recurring prize arenas operate, and Coefficient Giving still names sponsorship, incubation and large prizes as open gaps.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Several fiscal sponsors with AI safety sponsees (BERI, Ashgro, Rethink Priorities Special Projects) and shared-services providers such as Impact Ops; two operating incubators (Catalyze Impact and Constellation's incubator); recurring jailbreak and red-teaming arenas with cash prizes (Gray Swan) and occasional prize-backed competitions (CAIS, Apart Research, Humane Intelligence).
nodes.entry_points: To add capacity, join the operations team of an existing sponsor (Ashgro, Rethink Priorities Special Projects, BERI) or a shared-services provider such as Impact Ops. Would-be founders can apply to Catalyze Impact's or Constellation's incubator cohorts, both of which run open rounds. Gray Swan's arenas and Apart Research's sprints are open to anyone and sometimes pay prizes; a standing, large-prize programme for hard problems is the open gap that Coefficient Giving's 'Grand awards' initiative describes.

subareas.name: Talent and training
subareas.definition: The pipelines, matching mechanisms and support that move people into, through and up within AI safety, security and governance work, from first exposure to senior leadership, including ways to borrow scarce specialist expertise.
subareas.scope_rule: In: structural bottlenecks in moving people into and up within the field, and the infrastructure that could fix them. Out: course content and single programmes' operations; the research trained people go on to do.

nodes.name: Early-career pipeline capacity
nodes.definition: Early-career programmes (MATS, ARENA, SPAR, BlueDot, Pivotal, PIBBSS, ERA, CBAI, Iliad and others) have multiplied; Kairos and Constellation estimate that about 2,000 AI safety research fellows will be trained in 2026. The binding constraint is no longer applicant interest but the field's capacity to absorb them. Each senior researcher can mentor only a few people, and organisations mostly hire experienced people who need little supervision, so many graduates have nowhere to go next.
nodes.why_it_matters: If programmes grow faster than mentoring capacity and entry-level jobs, quality dilutes, graduates stall after their first fellowship, and the funding and goodwill that built the pipeline are wasted. Programmes also compete for the same mentors instead of dividing the work between them.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Programmes coordinate on who serves which stage and specialism, the number of people able and willing to mentor rises measurably, and most fellowship graduates move into safety roles or funded independent work within a year.

canonical_reference.title: AI Safety Talent Needs in 2026: Insights for Field-Building, MATS

nodes.boundary_notes: The structural bottleneck across early-career programmes, not a directory of them. Experienced career-changers are meta.talent.experienced-professionals; matching people to roles is meta.talent.matchmaking; senior and specialist hiring is meta.talent.senior-and-specialist-recruitment.
nodes.capacity_note: Many fellowships (MATS, ARENA, SPAR, BlueDot and others) are expected to train about 2,000 research fellows in 2026, but work on the binding constraint, mentor bandwidth and jobs for graduates, is limited to MATS's research and Kairos's coordination.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Some differentiation by format (bootcamp vs mentored research vs part-time), but largely unaddressed as a shared mentor-capacity problem across programmes.
nodes.entry_points: Newcomers should still start with MATS, ARENA or BlueDot's courses, with SPAR (run by Kairos) and Apart Research sprints as lower-commitment ways to test fit. For someone who wants to work on the bottleneck itself, the scarce contributions are mentoring, programme operations, and placing people after fellowships, which 80,000 Hours' fieldbuilding review names as neglected.

nodes.name: On-ramps for experienced professionals
nodes.definition: Experienced professionals (senior engineers, security specialists, policy veterans, operators) who want to move into AI safety have few structured on-ramps, and those already senior in adjacent fields lack the context, relationships and credibility to lead in this one; almost all fellowship infrastructure is built for students and early-career people.
nodes.why_it_matters: The field most needs people who already know how to build, secure and govern things, and it currently turns many of them away or leaves them on the margins.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Several well-run programmes that move experienced people into both staff and leadership roles each year, with a track record of placements.

nodes.boundary_notes: General on-ramps for experienced people. Active search for named senior specialists is meta.talent.senior-and-specialist-recruitment; early-career programmes are meta.talent.early-career-bottleneck.
nodes.capacity_note: SteadRise, Successif, Arcadia Impact and the Horizon Institute run programmes for experienced people, still a handful of small programmes against what Tailwind says is needed.
nodes.existing_mitigations: A small set of dedicated transition programmes (Successif, SteadRise, BlueDot's grants, the Generator Residency) that did not exist a few years ago.
nodes.entry_points: SteadRise is the most direct route for an experienced professional wanting a structured, one-to-one path in; Successif is the equivalent for people aiming specifically at AI governance. BlueDot's Career Transition Grant is a lighter-weight option for someone who already has a specific plan.

nodes.name: Senior and specialist capacity
nodes.definition: Safety organisations, frontier projects and lab safety teams struggle to get senior or narrowly specialised expertise, such as security engineers with the nation-state threat experience needed to reach RAND security levels SL4 and SL5, policy veterans with legislative drafting experience, or legal and technical specialists for a one-off question. Ordinary recruiting channels and pay do not reach these people, and small organisations cannot justify keeping every specialist on staff, so the field needs both a way to hire them and a way to borrow them on demand.
nodes.why_it_matters: Some of the most important gaps, weight security above all, cannot be filled by training newcomers, and without a shared pool of on-call experts every team either duplicates scarce hires or makes specialist decisions without specialist advice.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A dedicated search function and specialist pipelines, above all for security talent, fill senior and specialist roles within months, and a credible advisory body exists that safety teams, including small independent ones, routinely call on for specialist input.

canonical_reference.title: AI safety field-building survey: Talent needs, infrastructure needs, and relationship to EA (CEA, 2023)

key_agendas.name: Senior talent headhunting (Tailwind initiative)
Think tank for AI labs (Tailwind initiative)

nodes.boundary_notes: Getting scarce senior and specialist expertise into the field, by hiring it or borrowing it. Broad matching of people to roles is meta.talent.matchmaking; general on-ramps are meta.talent.experienced-professionals; the security work itself, and Tailwind's 'Security capacity buildout' initiative, sit with model.model-security.weights-security; the lab functions this expertise feeds are model.developer-assurance.
nodes.capacity_note: Impact Ops headhunts for high-impact organisations, Heron and security bootcamps build security pipelines, and GovAI, the Frontier Model Forum and METR supply advice informally, but nobody reliably finds nation-state-grade security engineers or runs an on-demand advisory service.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Impact Ops' recruitment and headhunting service; Heron, the AI Security Bootcamp and the Frontier AI Security Residency for security professionals; SteadRise introductions for leadership and operations roles; labs' own security recruiting. On the advisory side, GovAI, the Frontier Model Forum and METR each supply part of an on-demand function informally.
nodes.entry_points: A security specialist can join Heron's community or fellowship, or the AI Security Bootcamp, to build context and contacts; a senior policy or operations person can go through SteadRise. Someone who wants to build the missing capacity could join Impact Ops' AI-safety recruitment team, or pitch a dedicated search function or an on-demand advisory body to Coefficient Giving under its 'Senior talent headhunting' and 'Think tank for AI labs' initiatives.

nodes.name: Talent matchmaking
nodes.definition: With hundreds of organisations and a fragmented set of job boards, mailing lists and personal networks, a qualified person and a role that needs them frequently fail to find each other; Coefficient Giving names 'talent matchmaking' as a distinct gap even though 80,000 Hours, BlueDot and Kairos already do parts of this.
nodes.why_it_matters: Every unfilled role that could have been filled by an existing qualified person is a wasted opportunity cost on top of the field's stated talent bottleneck, and duplicated, incompatible matchmaking systems make it worse rather than better.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Important roles across the ecosystem are filled quickly by the best available person, because someone actively matches candidates to roles using shared talent directories and referrals, rather than relying on who happens to see a job advert.

canonical_reference.title: Talent matchmaking, Project Tailwind

key_agendas.name: Talent matchmaking (Tailwind initiative)

nodes.boundary_notes: Systematic matching of people to roles across the ecosystem. Bespoke search for senior and specialist people is meta.talent.senior-and-specialist-recruitment; people meeting in person is meta.convenings.convenings-and-events.
nodes.capacity_note: 80,000 Hours' job board and advising, BlueDot, Kairos and the AISafety.com jobs board each do part of this, without ecosystem-wide active matching.
nodes.existing_mitigations: 80,000 Hours' job board and advising line already provide a large, general-purpose matching mechanism; Kairos, BlueDot and Constellation each provide narrower, programme-specific matching.
nodes.entry_points: 80,000 Hours' job board and free 1-on-1 advising calls are the single most accessible entry point for anyone, regardless of experience level, looking to be matched to a role.

subareas.name: Evidence and strategy
subareas.definition: Cross-cutting research that gives the field a shared, up-to-date picture of AI capabilities, real-world harms and the state of knowledge on risk, and the strategic research that builds on it: explicit threat models, scenarios, and judgements about where effort should go.
subareas.scope_rule: In: evidence about capability trends, incidents and the state of knowledge on risk, its translation for decision-makers, and threat modelling, scenario work and field-level prioritisation as research outputs in their own right. Out: building any one evaluation (model.evaluations); detecting attacks as they happen (misuse.cyber.attack-detection); what alignment means conceptually (model.alignment.conceptual-foundations); the specific technical or policy research a strategy recommends.

nodes.name: Capability forecasting
nodes.definition: Estimating how fast AI capabilities, compute use and algorithmic efficiency will grow, and when specific dangerous capabilities are likely to arrive, so that safety and policy work can be sequenced against a realistic timeline rather than guesswork.
nodes.why_it_matters: Almost every other safety and governance decision (how urgently to fund something, when a regulation needs to bind, when a lab's safeguards need to be ready) depends on some implicit timeline; bad forecasts lead to safety work arriving after the capability it was meant to precede.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Forecasts of capability and compute trends are track-recorded, calibrated and specific enough that policymakers and safety researchers can cite a number with a stated confidence interval rather than a vibe.

canonical_reference.title: Trends in Artificial Intelligence, Epoch AI

key_agendas.name: Epoch AI trends
Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (task time horizons), METR
AI Futures Project timelines forecasting

nodes.boundary_notes: Producing forecasts of capability, compute and timelines. Using them for scenario reasoning is meta.evidence.macrostrategy-and-prioritisation; the benchmarks forecasts rest on are model.evaluations.benchmarks-and-tooling; economy-specific forecasting is society.economic-transition.labour-disruption.
nodes.capacity_note: Epoch AI, METR's time horizons, Metaculus, the Forecasting Research Institute and the AI Futures Project work on this with public track records.
nodes.entry_points: Metaculus is the lowest-friction way in: anyone can start forecasting AI questions today and build a public track record. Epoch AI and Forecasting Research Institute both list open roles and publish their methods openly, and the AI Futures Project is small enough that direct outreach with a concrete forecasting or scenario contribution is plausible.

nodes.name: Incident tracking
nodes.definition: A structured, ongoing record of AI-caused or AI-involved harms and near-misses (deployment failures, agent misbehaviour, misuse cases) that researchers, journalists and policymakers can query, analogous to aviation incident databases.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without a shared record, each new incident is analysed from scratch, patterns across incidents (which failure modes recur, which safeguards actually prevented harm) go unnoticed, and policy debates rely on anecdote rather than a queryable base rate.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A single widely-trusted incident database is comprehensive, current and used as a standard citation in policy and research documents, the way aviation's incident databases are used in that industry.

canonical_reference.title: Welcome to the Artificial Intelligence Incident Database

nodes.boundary_notes: The public catalogue of reported incidents. Investigating a specific incident's root cause is meta.evidence.incident-investigation; a lab's own disclosure is model.developer-assurance.incident-reporting; live detection of attacks is misuse.cyber.attack-detection.
nodes.capacity_note: The AI Incident Database, AIAAIC and the OECD's monitor maintain public catalogues, with frontier-model and agent incidents less well catalogued.
nodes.entry_points: The AI Incident Database accepts public incident submissions from anyone, the most direct way in. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor is a government-run tool rather than an entry route for individuals, but its methodology page is a good technical reference for anyone wanting to build a similar tracker.

nodes.name: Incident investigation
nodes.definition: When an AI system behaves dangerously or unexpectedly in the wild, someone needs to do the equivalent of an air-accident investigation: reconstruct what happened, why, and what would have prevented it, independently of the company whose system was involved.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without independent investigation, the public and other developers only get the account the involved company chooses to publish, which may understate causes uncomfortable for the company and misses lessons other developers need in order to avoid the same failure.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A recognised, resourced independent investigation capacity exists that can be triggered quickly after a significant incident and produces a public report with the credibility of, say, an aviation safety board.

canonical_reference.title: Brief independent investigation of agents' behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident, METR

key_agendas.name: AI incident investigations (Tailwind initiative)
How independent researchers could investigate AI propensities after misalignment incidents, METR

nodes.boundary_notes: Independent root-cause investigation of a specific incident, like an air-accident investigation. Whether a lab kept its promises is meta.watchdogs.lab-accountability; a lab's own disclosure is model.developer-assurance.incident-reporting; the catalogue of incidents is meta.evidence.incident-tracking.
nodes.capacity_note: The METR and Redwood Research investigation of the August 2026 OpenAI and Hugging Face incident is the first concrete example, a joint, ad hoc effort rather than a standing capacity.
nodes.entry_points: Coefficient Giving's Tailwind page names this a funding gap and explicitly invites teams to pitch a standing investigation capacity; METR and Redwood Research are both hiring and demonstrated exactly this kind of work in August 2026, making them the natural people to approach or apply to first.

nodes.name: Living reviews of AI risk
nodes.definition: A canonical, regularly updated synthesis of the evidence on AI risks (capability, misuse, misalignment, structural) that a policymaker or new researcher can read to get an accurate, current picture, rather than reconstructing it from scattered papers, blog posts and lab claims.
nodes.why_it_matters: Fragmented evidence means policymakers and new entrants either rely on whichever single source they encountered first (which may be outdated or one-sided) or spend large amounts of time reconstructing a synthesis that should be a shared public good.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A single or small number of reports are recognised across the field and by governments as the current best synthesis, updated on a predictable schedule, the way the IPCC reports function for climate science.

International AI Safety Report

nodes.boundary_notes: Synthesis of what is known about the risks. Synthesis of the field's own structure, and what to prioritise, is meta.evidence.macrostrategy-and-prioritisation; policy documents that use this evidence to argue for rules sit in society.public-policy.
nodes.capacity_note: The annual International AI Safety Report and the MIT AI Risk Repository exist, without a continuously updated synthesis of the kind Tailwind describes.

nodes.entry_points: The International AI Safety Report process periodically calls for nominated expert contributors through national governments, which is not a direct-application route; the MIT AI Risk Repository team and Coefficient Giving's Tailwind page are more approachable starting points for someone wanting to build or contribute to a living synthesis.

nodes.name: Capability demonstrations for decision-makers
nodes.definition: Producing clear, credible, hands-on demonstrations of specific dangerous or surprising frontier model capabilities (autonomous cyber intrusion, self-exfiltration, deception) for an audience of policymakers and executives who otherwise only see capabilities through a company's own marketing or a dry benchmark score.
nodes.why_it_matters: Abstract benchmark numbers rarely change minds the way a concrete, watchable demonstration does; without this translation layer, decision-makers underestimate or overestimate risk based on impressions rather than evidence.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Decision-makers routinely have access to credible, independently produced demonstrations of current frontier capabilities before making major policy or investment decisions, rather than relying solely on lab-provided materials.

canonical_reference.title: Shutdown Resistance in Reasoning Models, Palisade Research

key_agendas.name: Frontier capabilities observatory (Tailwind initiative)

nodes.boundary_notes: Translating results into hands-on demonstrations for decision-makers. The measurement is model.evaluations.dangerous-capability-evals; bio-specific demonstrations for policymakers sit with misuse.bio-chem.knowledge-uplift; material for the general public is meta.communications.public-explanation.
nodes.capacity_note: Palisade Research and CivAI show demonstrations to lawmakers and AI Digest builds interactive explainers, without a systematic, regularly updated view across capability areas.
nodes.entry_points: Palisade Research publishes its methods openly and is the clearest model to emulate or join; Coefficient Giving's Tailwind page is actively looking to fund a dedicated 'observatory' along these lines, so a concrete proposal is a plausible route to funding.

nodes.name: Threat modelling
nodes.definition: Systematically developing, comparing and curating explicit models of how catastrophic outcomes from AI could actually occur (which actors, which failure chains, which warning signs), as a discipline in its own right rather than an implicit assumption buried inside individual papers and proposals.
nodes.why_it_matters: Different organisations currently operate on different, often unstated threat models, which makes it hard to compare the relative value of their work or spot a threat model that most of the field has neglected entirely.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A small number of institutions maintain and continuously update rigorous, explicit, comparable threat models that most of the field references, the way biosecurity has established threat-modelling conventions for pandemic risk.

canonical_reference.title: An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks (Hendrycks, Mazeika and Woodside, 2023)

key_agendas.name: Threat modeling institute (Tailwind initiative)

nodes.boundary_notes: Modelling the causal paths to catastrophe as a discipline. Specific mechanisms are nodes in society.structural-risk and the Harmful use layer; scenario work and judgements about where effort should go are meta.evidence.macrostrategy-and-prioritisation; what alignment means is model.alignment.conceptual-foundations.
nodes.capacity_note: Forethought and Convergence Analysis do closely related work and labs publish risk taxonomies, but nobody maintains explicit, comparable threat models as a main mandate.
nodes.entry_points: Forethought and Convergence Analysis both publish their research programmes openly and are realistic direct-application or collaboration targets; Coefficient Giving's Tailwind page is explicitly seeking a founder to build a dedicated institute around this function.

nodes.name: Macrostrategy and prioritisation
nodes.definition: Research that builds integrated scenarios of how transformative AI could unfold and uses them, together with evidence about the field itself, to judge which interventions, organisations and gaps deserve scarce money and talent. Scenario work stress-tests strategy rather than producing a single forecast; prioritisation compares interventions and studies the field as an ecosystem (which sub-problems are neglected, how organisations divide the work, how growth should be sequenced).
nodes.why_it_matters: Point forecasts do not tell anyone what to do differently, and with scarce money and talent, misjudging which gaps matter most wastes years; without scenario work and field-level study, gaps like the empty nodes on this map stay invisible.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Several independent groups produce falsifiable scenario work that is revisited against what actually happens, and regular, public, evidence-based prioritisation of the field's gaps is used by funders and entrants, with this map aiming to be one input.

nodes.boundary_notes: Scenario reasoning and deciding where effort should go. Calibrated forecasts of measurable trends are meta.evidence.capability-forecasting; synthesis of what is known about the risks is meta.evidence.state-of-risk; explicit models of how catastrophes could unfold are meta.evidence.threat-modelling; moving money is meta.funding; economy-specific scenarios are society.economic-transition.labour-disruption.
nodes.capacity_note: A few small, well-regarded groups build scenarios (the AI Futures Project, Forethought) and several organisations prioritise as part of wider mandates (Coefficient Giving, 80,000 Hours, Arb Research's shallow review).
nodes.entry_points: The AI Futures Project and Forethought both publish openly and are the natural first stops for scenario work. RAND's AI and emerging-risk teams offer a more institutional route for someone with a policy or defence background. For prioritisation, 80,000 Hours' career review and job board is the most accessible entry point and is kept current, and Coefficient Giving's Tailwind page is a public list of prioritised gaps that doubles as a funding pitch for anyone wanting to found something in one of them.

subareas.name: Watchdogs and accountability
subareas.definition: Independent organisations that scrutinise AI developers' safety claims and practices from outside, without needing the developer's cooperation, and support for insiders who speak out.
subareas.scope_rule: In: independent outside scrutiny of AI developers that needs no cooperation from them, and practical support for whistleblowers. Out: audits a developer takes part in and the supply of auditors (model.developer-assurance.third-party-auditing); whistleblower law and regulatory enforcement (society.public-policy).

nodes.name: Lab accountability tracking
nodes.definition: Independent, recurring public ratings that compare frontier AI companies on safety practice, and ongoing tracking of changes to their published safety policies that flags when a promise is quietly weakened.
nodes.why_it_matters: Without outside scrutiny, commitments can be walked back unnoticed and the public, investors and regulators cannot compare developers.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Sustained, well-funded scorecards and change-tracking covering all major developers, cited by regulators, investors and journalists.

canonical_reference.title: AI Safety Index: Summer 2026, Future of Life Institute

key_agendas.name: Frontier lab accountability (Tailwind initiative)

nodes.boundary_notes: Outside scrutiny that needs no cooperation from the lab. The commitments being scored are model.developer-assurance.frontier-safety-frameworks; audits with privileged access are model.developer-assurance.third-party-auditing; investigating a specific incident is meta.evidence.incident-investigation.
nodes.capacity_note: SaferAI, Guidelight, the Midas Project, FLI and Stanford's Foundation Model Transparency Index publish recurring comparisons of lab safety practice.
nodes.entry_points: SaferAI, Guidelight and the Midas Project are small teams that publish their methods and are realistic outreach targets for someone wanting to contribute research or software to a scorecard or policy tracker. Anyone joining should know that AI Lab Watch, the best-known one-person scorecard, closed in September 2025, which shows the main risk in this space: keeping the work going.

nodes.name: Whistleblower support
nodes.definition: Legal, financial and reputational support for employees of AI companies who want to raise safety concerns externally, separate from any internal reporting channel the company itself provides.
nodes.why_it_matters: Internal-only reporting channels give a company control over which concerns become public; independent whistleblower support is what allows genuinely inconvenient information to reach regulators, journalists or the public when internal channels fail or are not trusted.
nodes.progress_looks_like: AI company employees with safety-relevant concerns know of, and can access, independent legal and practical support for coming forward, comparable to whistleblower protection infrastructure in finance or aviation.

canonical_reference.title: The AI Whistleblower Initiative (AIWI)

nodes.boundary_notes: Practical legal, financial and reputational support from outside the company. Legal protection in statute is society.public-policy.whistleblower-protection; internal channels are model.developer-assurance.internal-safety-governance.
nodes.capacity_note: The AI Whistleblower Initiative is the one organisation dedicated to AI insiders, with general tech whistleblower groups (Psst.org, Whistleblower Aid, The Signals Network, the National Whistleblower Center) also helping.
nodes.entry_points: AIWI's site is the direct route for AI company insiders with a concern, and for professionals who want to join the expert network behind its 'Third Opinion' service. Lawyers and investigators can also volunteer with general tech whistleblower groups such as Psst.org or Whistleblower Aid, which take AI cases.

subareas.name: Communications and public engagement
subareas.definition: The journalism, polling, message research, advocacy and explanatory work that shapes what the public, media and non-specialist decision-makers understand and believe about AI risk.
subareas.scope_rule: In: measuring, informing and shaping public and media understanding of AI risk. Out: the research being communicated, and the laws that result (society.public-policy).

nodes.name: Public opinion and message research
nodes.definition: Systematic research on what the public and particular constituencies think about AI risk and regulation, and on how they respond to different ways of describing it: rigorous, repeated polling on one side, and audience research and message testing on the other. Covers the overall picture that the field's many communicators create, as opposed to occasional surveys run for one campaign's needs.
nodes.why_it_matters: Policymakers and advocates routinely make claims about what the public wants on AI without reliable evidence, and well-meaning messages from different organisations can add up to a confusing or self-undermining picture; measured opinion and tested framing let the field see both.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A few recognised, methodologically transparent, longitudinal series track opinion on AI risk and regulation across major countries, communicators share tested evidence on which framings inform rather than polarise, and independent research shows public understanding becoming more stable and accurate over time.

canonical_reference.title: How the US Public and AI Experts View Artificial Intelligence, Pew Research Center (April 2025)

key_agendas.name: From Catastrophic to Concrete: message testing on AI risk (Seismic Foundation and co-authors, 2025)

nodes.boundary_notes: Measuring what the public thinks and testing how it responds. Campaigning to change opinion or policy is meta.communications.advocacy; explaining AI risk to the public is meta.communications.public-explanation; the resulting policy debate is society.public-policy.
nodes.capacity_note: Established pollsters run recurring AI attitude surveys and AIPI and Seismic Foundation commission AI-risk polling and message testing, without neutral, consistent tracking of questions on catastrophic risk and frontier regulation.
nodes.owner_field: survey research and public opinion polling
nodes.connection_note: Pollsters' own AI series rarely ask about catastrophic risk or frontier regulation, and AI safety organisations' polling is mostly advocacy-aligned; what should flow is consistent, neutral questions into established series and shared evidence on framing across communicators.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Established pollsters' recurring series on attitudes to AI (Pew, Gallup, YouGov, Ipsos's AI Monitor, the UK government's public attitudes tracker); AIPI's recurring US polls; Seismic Foundation's audience research and narrative-strategy support for other organisations; informal coordination among communicators through venues such as The Curve and Constellation.
nodes.entry_points: Someone with survey skills can do most by getting consistent questions on catastrophic risk and regulation into existing series, through partnerships with Pew, YouGov or Ipsos, or by building a neutral tracker outside the US. AIPI and Seismic Foundation both commission research and are small enough to approach directly, and Seismic publishes its message-testing work openly.

nodes.name: Explaining AI risk to the public
nodes.definition: Journalism and standing explanatory material (explainers, FAQs, accessible summaries) that accurately translate AI safety and governance research for people with no background, as opposed to material written for people already planning to enter the field.
nodes.why_it_matters: Public and political understanding of AI risk is shaped mostly by generalist coverage that oscillates between hype and dismissal; without accurate translation, good research does not reach the people who vote and legislate.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Specialist reporters and well-maintained general-audience explainers that are widely read outside the already-engaged community.

canonical_reference.title: AISafety.info

nodes.boundary_notes: Explaining to the public. The underlying synthesis is meta.evidence.state-of-risk; demonstrations for decision-makers are meta.evidence.capability-demonstrations; campaigning for a position is meta.communications.advocacy.
nodes.capacity_note: Explainers for the already curious (AISafety.info, 80,000 Hours' AI in Context, AI Digest) and outlets aimed at the public and press (Tarbell's newsroom fellows, The AI Safety Foundation), while most mainstream AI coverage comes from reporters without a safety specialism.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Transformer's daily coverage, AISafety.info's FAQ database, and a handful of individual explainer projects.
nodes.entry_points: Tarbell Center's annual fellowship is the most structured route into AI journalism specifically. AISafety.info takes volunteer contributors and welcomes GitHub pull requests for its explainer database, and is the lowest-friction way to start writing public-facing AI safety explanations without founding anything new.

nodes.name: Advocacy
nodes.definition: Organisations that campaign directly for public and political action on catastrophic AI risk, from grassroots protest movements to Washington-style legislative advocacy shops, distinct from research organisations that merely publish findings.
nodes.why_it_matters: Research findings do not become policy on their own; sustained public and political pressure is usually needed to move legislation. That pressure now meets well-funded opposition, including industry-backed super PACs formed in 2025 to fight state AI safety laws. On the safety side, campaigning is done by a few young organisations whose tactics, from street protest to formal lobbying, are themselves debated within the field.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Advocacy organisations exist with a track record of moving specific, named legislation or regulatory decisions, and enough diversity of tactic and constituency that the field is not dependent on one approach or one country's political dynamics.

canonical_reference.title: ControlAI

nodes.boundary_notes: Campaigning for public and political action. The laws campaigned for are society.public-policy.legislation; measuring opinion and testing messages is meta.communications.public-opinion; advocacy on bias sits with society.ethics-fairness-welfare.fairness-and-bias.
nodes.capacity_note: Several organisations use different tactics (PauseAI, ControlAI, ARI, Encode, FLI, MIRI), while industry-funded counter-advocacy has grown faster since 2025.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Direct policymaker engagement (ControlAI, Encode), public protest (PauseAI), large-scale campaigning (FLI), and trade-published public argument (MIRI's book).
nodes.entry_points: PauseAI and ControlAI both explicitly recruit volunteers for protests and constituent meetings with almost no entry barrier; Encode and FLI both list open roles and internships for people wanting paid advocacy work. Someone wanting a lower-commitment start could join a PauseAI local chapter or ControlAI's campaign email list.

subareas.name: Convenings and coordination
subareas.definition: The events, venues and dialogue infrastructure that let people working on AI safety, security and governance across organisations, sectors and countries find each other, build trust and coordinate.
subareas.scope_rule: In: the infrastructure for bringing people together, whatever the topic. Out: the content discussed, and dialogue between countries' research and policy communities (society.international-governance.great-power-dialogue).

nodes.name: Convenings and events
nodes.definition: The recurring events and shared event infrastructure that bring people working on AI safety, security and governance together: cross-sector gatherings of lab staff, officials, academics, journalists and civil society; focused forums for one technical or policy subfield; and the venues, logistics and event-running capacity that let any organisation host these without rebuilding that capacity each time.
nodes.why_it_matters: Papers and briefs are slow to build the trust and shared context that coordination between labs, governments and civil society needs, young subfields develop slowly when practitioners cannot compare notes, and the small organisations that would benefit most from convening often lack the capacity to run a good event.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Enough well-run convenings exist, at different scales and specificities, that key relationships do not depend on a single annual guest list; every growing subfield has a recurring forum of its own; and any funded organisation can use shared venues and event support anywhere, not only in one city.

canonical_reference.title: Reflections on The Curve, Second Thoughts

key_agendas.name: Cross-sector convenings (Tailwind initiative)
Subfield forums (Tailwind initiative)
Events as a service (Tailwind initiative)

nodes.boundary_notes: Bringing people together, whatever the topic, through events and the infrastructure behind them. Place-based communities outside the main hubs are meta.convenings.regional-hubs; dialogue between countries' research and policy communities, including IDAIS, is society.international-governance.great-power-dialogue; government summits sit in society.international-governance; the technical content belongs to the relevant node in another layer.
nodes.capacity_note: Recurring subfield forums (ControlConf, the AI Security Forum, the Alignment Workshop series), a few cross-sector gatherings (The Curve, the Athens Roundtable) and one strong shared venue (Lighthaven), with no general events service usable anywhere.
nodes.existing_mitigations: The Curve and The Future Society's Athens Roundtable bring sectors together; ControlConf, the AI Security Forum, FAR.AI's Alignment Workshop series and the ILIAD conferences serve particular subfields, alongside workshops at ICML and NeurIPS; Lighthaven offers a venue and event-running experience, and LISA and Constellation host events for their communities.
nodes.entry_points: The Alignment Workshop and ControlConf take external applications and are the standard first technical events for someone entering control or alignment research, and the AI Security Forum is the equivalent for people from a security background. Cross-sector gatherings such as The Curve are invitation-based, so the practical route is to build a track record at open events first. An organisation wanting to run an event can book Lighthaven; someone wanting to build the general 'events as a service' capacity Coefficient Giving describes would be filling a named gap.

nodes.name: Regional community hubs
nodes.definition: Physical or organisational hubs (shared offices, local meetup networks, national chapters) that let AI safety researchers and newcomers in a given city or country find each other and collaborate, as opposed to the field being concentrated in Berkeley, London and a few other hub cities.
nodes.why_it_matters: Talent and useful perspectives exist outside the existing hub cities, especially in the Global South, but without local infrastructure they stay disconnected from the wider field and the field itself misses regional context it needs (e.g. how AI risk plays out in a different regulatory or economic setting).
nodes.progress_looks_like: Active, self-sustaining local hubs exist in a much wider set of cities and countries, each connected into the wider field rather than isolated, and specifically including hubs in the Global South alongside the existing North American and European concentration.

canonical_reference.title: AI safety communities worldwide, AISafety.com

nodes.boundary_notes: Place-based community infrastructure outside the main hub cities. Individual career pipelines are meta.talent; participation of the same regions in global governance is society.international-governance.inclusive-participation.
nodes.capacity_note: Outside Berkeley and London, small national and regional groups (ENAIS, CeSIA, AIGS Canada, Singapore, South Africa, ILINA, India, Brazil) run hubs with few paid staff, and much of Latin America, the Middle East and South and Southeast Asia has little.
nodes.existing_mitigations: LISA and Constellation as the two main physical hubs; ENAIS, ILINA and national groups as newer regional infrastructure.
nodes.entry_points: LISA and Constellation both run fellowship or visiting-researcher programmes that are the standard route to a desk in the two main hub cities. Someone outside Berkeley or London is better served starting with ENAIS (Europe) or ILINA (Africa), both of which actively recruit through their own programmes rather than requiring relocation.

subareas.name: Research tooling and public goods
subareas.definition: Shared, non-rival resources (compute, datasets and environments, and AI assistance for research) that lower the cost of doing safety and governance research for anyone in the ecosystem rather than any single organisation.
subareas.scope_rule: In: shared resources that lower the cost of safety research. Out: evaluation benchmarks and harnesses (model.evaluations.benchmarks-and-tooling); decision tools for governments and boards (society.epistemics.decision-quality); rules on who may access compute (society.compute-governance); the findings produced with these resources.

nodes.name: Shared compute, data and environments
nodes.definition: Shared compute (GPU clusters, cloud credits, remote access to the internals of large open models) and public datasets and test environments built to advance safety research, available to nonprofit and academic researchers who cannot build their own. Frontier labs have all of these in-house; outside them, empirical safety research is limited by what researchers can buy, borrow or rebuild from scratch.
nodes.why_it_matters: If independent researchers cannot get the compute, model access and environments that lab teams take for granted, safety research outside the labs is capped at small models and duplicated effort, and the field's independent check on lab claims weakens.
nodes.progress_looks_like: A dedicated, adequately sized compute resource for safety research exists, alongside maintained public libraries of safety-specific datasets and environments that any researcher can use, as ControlArena now is for control research.

canonical_reference.title: Compute Cluster, Center for AI Safety

key_agendas.name: Compute cluster for AI safety (Tailwind initiative)
Datasets for AI safety (Tailwind initiative)
ControlArena, UK AI Security Institute's open library of control environments

nodes.boundary_notes: Shared compute, data and environments for safety research. Benchmarks and harnesses built to measure models are model.evaluations.benchmarks-and-tooling; government rules on who can access compute are society.compute-governance; AI tools that speed up research are meta.tooling.ai-uplift.
nodes.capacity_note: The CAIS compute cluster (closed to new applicants), NDIF's access to open-model internals and open environment libraries such as ControlArena exist, but nothing operates at the scale Tailwind describes.
nodes.existing_mitigations: The CAIS compute cluster (paused for new applicants); NDIF for remote access to the internals of open models; open environment libraries that come out of individual research programmes (ControlArena, CAIS datasets such as WMDP, Redwood's control settings); commercial environment-building for frontier labs (Trajectory Labs), which is related but not a public good; general national and commercial compute programmes with nothing earmarked for safety.
nodes.entry_points: Researchers can contact CAIS about future access to its cluster, use NDIF for interpretability work on large open models, or apply to general schemes (NAIRR, Isambard-AI, Lambda, Prime Intellect). Contributors can add to open environment libraries such as ControlArena, which accept outside contributions, or build a dataset for a named gap. Someone with infrastructure experience could build the larger shared cluster Coefficient Giving says it wants to fund.

nodes.name: AI uplift for safety research
nodes.definition: Deliberately applying current frontier AI capabilities (coding assistance, literature synthesis, experiment automation) to speed up AI safety research itself, so that the safety ecosystem benefits from capability progress rather than being structurally slower than capabilities work that has no qualms about heavy AI-assisted development.
nodes.why_it_matters: If capabilities research increasingly uses AI to accelerate itself while safety research does not, the gap between how fast capabilities and safety progress will widen for a reason that has nothing to do with the intrinsic difficulty of either.
nodes.progress_looks_like: Independent safety organisations routinely and effectively use frontier AI tools to accelerate their research pipelines, with measurable productivity gains comparable to what capabilities labs report internally.

canonical_reference.title: Automated Alignment Researchers, Anthropic

key_agendas.name: AI uplift for AI safety (Tailwind initiative)

nodes.boundary_notes: The independent ecosystem adopting frontier AI for its own work. Frontier labs' plan to automate alignment research, and the problem of trusting its output, is model.alignment.automated-alignment-research; measuring AI research capability is model.evaluations; AI tools for policy decisions are society.epistemics.decision-quality.
nodes.capacity_note: Transluce builds AI research tools that other safety teams use, and labs automate their own research internally, but no programme helps the independent ecosystem adopt frontier tools.
nodes.existing_mitigations: Anthropic's internal automated-alignment-researcher pipeline; ad hoc use of general coding/research assistants by independent researchers, not organised as a programme.
nodes.entry_points: Transluce publishes its tools and hires research engineers, and independent researchers can adopt Docent and similar tools now. Someone who wants to close the gap could give the ecosystem shared agent scaffolds, model credits and training, which is what Coefficient Giving's Tailwind initiative asks for.
